0.title: Zechariah: Behold, Your King Is Coming
0.overview:
The message. Zechariah speaks to a small, tired people who have come home from exile to a ruined city and an unfinished temple, and tells them that God has come home too: “Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you” (1:3). He has not finished with them. He will clean away their sin, live in their midst and bring the nations to worship him, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (4:6). At the centre of his plan stands a coming King who is also a Priest: he rides into Zion on a donkey, is valued at thirty pieces of silver, is pierced and struck down, and opens a fountain that washes sin away. The book begins on a building site and ends on the day when “the LORD will be king over all the earth” (14:9).

Background: the writer. Zechariah, whose name means “the LORD remembers”, was the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (1:1). Iddo headed one of the priestly families that came back from Babylon (Nehemiah 12:4, 16), so the prophet was very likely a priest too, which fits his deep interest in the temple, the high priest and cleansing. Ezra names him beside Haggai as the two prophets through whose preaching the temple was rebuilt (Ezra 5:1; 6:14).

When and where. In about 538 BC Cyrus of Persia let the exiles of Judah go home. Some fifty thousand returned (Ezra 2:64–65) under Zerubbabel, the governor, a descendant of David, and Joshua the high priest. They laid the temple’s foundation, but opposition, poor harvests and their own houses drained their zeal, and the work stopped for some sixteen years, “until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia” (Ezra 4:24). That was 520 BC. Haggai began to preach in the late summer, Zechariah two months later (1:1). His dated messages run to about 518 BC (7:1), and the temple was finished in about 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Judah was a tiny province of a vast empire, with no king on David’s throne; God’s great promises seemed to have shrunk to almost nothing.

The kind of writing. Chapters 1–6 are eight visions seen in one night: horses, horns, a lampstand, a flying scroll, a woman in a basket. They are pictures, not puzzles, and an angel explains each one, so listen to the explanation rather than decode every detail. Chapters 9–14 are two oracles (9:1; 12:1), mostly poetry, which look far beyond Zechariah’s day. Like a traveller who sees distant mountain ranges as one skyline, they set near events and the end of history side by side.

How the book makes its case. A call to repent and not repeat the fathers’ mistakes (1:1–6) opens the night visions (1:7–6:8). God declares himself jealous for his ruined city; the powers that scattered Judah are cast down; Jerusalem will spill beyond its walls, with God as “a wall of fire all around” (2:5). At the centre, Joshua the high priest, accused by Satan, is stripped of his filthy garments and clothed in clean ones (chapter 3), and Zerubbabel is promised that the Spirit will finish what he began (chapter 4). Then sin is carried out of the land (chapter 5), and a crown set on Joshua’s head points to “the man whose name is the Branch” (6:9–15). In chapters 7–8 a question about fasting draws out God’s call to justice and mercy and a run of promises: children playing in Jerusalem’s streets, and the nations saying, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you” (8:23). The first oracle (chapters 9–11) announces the coming King, then tells of the good shepherd whom the flock rejects. The second (chapters 12–14) shows Jerusalem besieged and rescued, the people mourning the one they pierced, a fountain for sin, the shepherd struck, and the LORD reigning over all. The book moves from small beginnings, through rejection and cleansing, to a kingdom that fills the world.

One prophet or two? Many scholars think chapters 9–14 come from a later writer: the dates and visions disappear, the style changes, Greece is named (9:13), and the march of judgment in 9:1–8 recalls Alexander the Great’s campaign down the coast in 332 BC. Others reply that a change of subject explains a change of style; that the Greeks were already known in the Persian age; and that both halves share themes such as the cleansing of the land and the coming of the nations. This commentary’s view: the book is the work of one prophet, though believing scholars still debate it, and the New Testament quotes both halves as Scripture.

How should chapter 14 be read? Premillennial and dispensational readers expect a literal fulfilment centred on Jerusalem, with an earthly reign of Christ after his return. Much of the Reformed tradition reads the besieged city as God’s people assaulted by the world to the end and rescued by God, and the living waters and worshipping nations as Christ’s reign now, completed in the new creation. This commentary takes the second, amillennial view, because Revelation takes up Zechariah’s river and the end of every curse for the new creation: “No longer will there be anything accursed” (Revelation 22:3). Others hold their view from the same Scriptures in good faith, and all agree that Christ will return bodily, judge the nations and reign.

Where it leads: to Christ. Zechariah points to Christ above all by direct promise, which the Gospels draw on in the story of his death. As Jesus rode into Jerusalem, Matthew heard 9:9: “Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey” (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). On the night of his arrest Jesus applied 13:7 to himself: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matthew 26:31). The thirty pieces of silver thrown into the house of the LORD (11:12–13) became the price of his betrayal (Matthew 27:9–10). At the cross John saw 12:10 fulfilled: “They will look on him whom they have pierced” (John 19:37). There is pattern too: Joshua, cleansed and crowned, is a sign of the Branch who is priest and king at once (3:8; 6:13). Above all, the book shows who God is. The LORD says, “when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced” (12:10); the shepherd his sword strikes is “the man who stands next to me” (13:7); and the angel of the LORD, sent by the LORD yet speaking as the LORD (1:12; 2:8–11), this commentary takes to be the Son before his incarnation. From far off Zechariah sees God himself coming to live among his people, pierced for them, and opening “a fountain … to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness” (13:1). The New Testament names that fountain: “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

For us. Zechariah is a book for anyone serving God in a day of small things. The work may be slow, but “whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice” (4:10), because the work is God’s and done by his Spirit. When the accuser points to our filthy garments, we need not argue our case: the LORD rebukes him, takes our iniquity away and clothes us himself (3:1–4), because Christ has borne it. Our King came humble, and he still calls the far-off home. And the last scene shapes ordinary days: “Holy to the LORD”, once engraved on the high priest’s turban, is written on the bells of horses, and every cooking pot is as holy as the bowls at the altar (14:20–21). Under Christ no corner of life lies outside God’s claim, and nothing done for him in the smallest place is wasted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls a new generation back to himself, and promises to come back to them. The section opens with an uncomfortable fact: the LORD was very angry with their fathers, and the exile was his doing (vv. 1–2). Yet the first word to the children is invitation, “Return to me … and I will return to you” (v. 3). Then a warning drawn from history: the fathers would not listen to the former prophets (v. 4); fathers and prophets alike are dead, but God’s words outlived them and overtook them, until in exile they admitted he had dealt with them exactly as he said (vv. 5–6). Believe God’s word now, rather than learn the hard way.
verseByVerse.theology: God's call to a new generation is to learn from the last one, because his word outlives everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying, "The LORD was very angry with your fathers. Therefore say to them, Thus declares the LORD of hosts: Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has been rightly angry with his people’s fathers, but his first word to their children is an invitation: come back to me, and I will come back to you.

In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius. Autumn 520 BC, two months after Haggai began (Haggai 1:1; see the introduction). Ezra names them together: “the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah” (Ezra 5:1). Haggai was the site foreman, urging the work on; Zechariah is the visionary, lifting their eyes to what God is doing behind the scenes and centuries ahead.

The LORD was very angry with your fathers. The exile was not an accident of politics but God’s anger against a persistently unfaithful people.

Return to me. The heart of the chapter is an invitation, and the order matters. God does not say “clean yourselves up and then come”. He says come, and I will come. Malachi would repeat it (Malachi 3:7), and James puts it in New Testament words: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8).

I will return to you. “Says the LORD of hosts”, three times in one verse: this is the commander of heaven’s armies speaking. And he does not merely offer to restore their fortunes or rebuild their walls; he offers himself, the best thing he ever gives. In the end he came back in person, in his Son, and keeps the way home open, “for he will abundantly pardon” (Isaiah 55:7).

How do I return? Admit the drift. Prayer thinned out, church became optional, a habit you once fought you now excuse: name it to God in plain words. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Do not wait until you feel ready. You do not have to repair the damage first. Turn round in something specific. Open the Bible tonight, go back to church on Sunday, make the apology, end what you have been hiding. Refuse the family pattern. “Do not be like your fathers” (v. 4): whatever you inherited from a home where God did not count need not be yours.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah was probably of a priestly family (Neh 12:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, Return from your evil ways and from your evil deeds.' But they did not hear or pay attention to me, declares the LORD. Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever? But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? So they repented and said, 'As the LORD of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fathers ignored God’s prophets and learned the hard way that his word comes true; their children are called to believe it now. Fathers and prophets have died, but God’s word has outlived them all.

Do not be like your fathers. Zechariah’s hearers had inherited the wreckage of their grandparents’ choices, and inheriting the consequences does not automatically mean learning the lesson. The former prophets, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah, had called, “Return from your evil ways”, and been ignored.

Your fathers, where are they? The fathers are dead, and so are the prophets. Everyone in that old argument is gone, but God’s words remain and “overtake” people, like a pursuer who catches up in the end. Jesus said the same of his own words: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

So has he dealt with us. In exile the fathers finally admitted God had been right. A grim way to be persuaded: Zechariah’s hearers are invited to believe God’s word now, rather than be convinced later by seeing it come true. And the God who overtook their fathers in judgment is now calling them home with mercy (v. 3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — The Horseman Among the Myrtles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the world is comfortable and God’s people are not, God is neither blind nor indifferent. In a night vision a rider on a red horse stands among the myrtles in a hollow, with other horses behind him (vv. 7–8). They are God’s patrol, and they report that all the earth is at rest: the empires are secure while Jerusalem lies in ruins (vv. 9–11). The angel of the LORD asks how long God will withhold mercy (v. 12), and the answer is gracious and comforting words (v. 13): God is jealous for Jerusalem, angry with nations that made her suffering worse, and has returned with mercy, so his house and his cities will be rebuilt (vv. 14–17).
verseByVerse.theology: When the world is comfortable and God's people are not, God is neither asleep nor indifferent.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying, "I saw in the night, and behold, a man riding on a red horse! He was standing among the myrtle trees in the glen, and behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses. Then I said, 'What are these, my lord?' The angel who talked with me said to me, 'I will show you what they are.' So the man who was standing among the myrtle trees answered, 'These are they whom the LORD has sent to patrol the earth.' And they answered the angel of the LORD who was standing among the myrtle trees, and said, 'We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth remains at rest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first night vision God’s scouts report that the whole world is at peace, and that, while Jerusalem lies in ruins, is exactly the problem. God sees everything happening on earth, even when his people feel forgotten.

I saw in the night. Three months later comes a series of eight night visions, running to 6:8. Strange, vivid and hopeful, they were given to people on a building site with little to encourage them (see the introduction).

Among the myrtle trees in the glen. A rider on a red horse stands among myrtles, low, bushy, fragrant shrubs, in a hollow, with other horses behind him. The scene is quiet and ordinary, as God’s activity often is. Three figures appear: the rider, called “the man” and then “the angel of the LORD” (vv. 10–11); the horsemen behind him; and “the angel who talked with me”, the interpreter who explains the visions to Zechariah.

What are these, my lord? Zechariah keeps asking all through the visions, and is never rebuked: honest questions are welcome.

To patrol the earth. Like a king’s scouts reporting back from the provinces. God is not uninformed about what is happening in Persia or anywhere else.

All the earth remains at rest. It sounds like good news, but it is the problem. The great empires are comfortable and secure while God’s people struggle in a ruined city. Haggai had promised that God would shake the nations (Haggai 2:6–7), and nothing is shaking. The timing fits: Darius had spent his first years crushing revolts across the empire, and by early 519 BC, when this vision came, the Persian world had settled into an untroubled calm.

When heaven seems quiet. Believers know this feeling: the wicked untroubled, the church small and tired, heaven silent. The next verse speaks to exactly that moment.

Where Christians differ. Who is the rider among the myrtles? Verse 11 calls him the angel of the LORD, and he intercedes for Jerusalem (v. 12). Some take him as a created angel speaking for God; many in the Reformed tradition see the Son before his incarnation, interceding for God’s people as he does now (Hebrews 7:25).

This commentary’s view. The second reading is the more likely. Elsewhere the angel of the LORD speaks and acts as God himself, and in Zechariah he is sent by the LORD yet speaks as the LORD (2:8–11).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “glen” usually means “the depths”, often of the sea; here it is probably a low, shaded hollow, though some think it hints at the deep places of the world. The colour translated “sorrel” is rare and may mean reddish-brown or bay (older versions read “speckled”). The vision does not explain the colours, so it is wise not to build on them.
verseByVerse.note: The first of eight night visions (1:7–6:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel of the LORD said, 'O LORD of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry these seventy years?' And the LORD answered gracious and comforting words to the angel who talked with me. So the angel who talked with me said to me, 'Cry out, Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cry “how long?” is taken up in heaven itself, and God answers it with comfort: he is passionately committed to his people.

How long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem? The exiles’ prayer of seventy years is put to God by one who stands in his presence, the angel of the LORD.

These seventy years. The span Jeremiah had foretold (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10); counted from the temple’s destruction in 586 BC, it was nearly up. God keeps his calendar precisely, even when his people cannot see the clock.

Gracious and comforting words. God does not rebuke the question. Anyone praying through a long disappointment may take heart.

I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem. Not petty envy but a husband’s fierce, protective love, which cannot stand by while his wife is harmed.

The prayer still prayed in heaven. If the angel of the LORD is the Son before his coming, this is a glimpse of the work he still does. Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and the Spirit prays within us when we do not know what to ask (Romans 8:26). When your own prayers run dry, his do not.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease; for while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster. Therefore, thus says the LORD, I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy; my house shall be built in it, declares the LORD of hosts, and the measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem. Cry out again, Thus says the LORD of hosts: My cities shall again overflow with prosperity, and the LORD will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is angry with the nations that went beyond his discipline and enjoyed his people’s ruin, and he has come back to Jerusalem with mercy to rebuild.

Exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease. The comfortable calm of verse 11 has not escaped his notice.

They furthered the disaster. The charge is precise: “while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster”. God used them to discipline his people, and they went far beyond what he gave them to do, enjoying the destruction (compare Isaiah 47:6). Being an instrument in God’s hand is no excuse for cruelty.

I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy. The promise answers verse 3. They were told “Return to me”; now God says he has already returned. A measuring line comes out, which is what builders do when they mean to build (the next vision picks it up, 2:1–5). And three times “again”: prosperity again, comfort again, chosen again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — Four Horns and Four Craftsmen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every power that scatters God’s people has a match, sent by God to break it. Zechariah sees four horns, pictures of power in every direction, and is told they are the nations that scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem (vv. 18–19). Then God shows him four craftsmen, workmen with tools, and explains that they have come to terrify those horns and cast them down, because the horns crushed his people so that no one could lift his head (vv. 20–21). The number matches exactly: God is never one short.
verseByVerse.theology: For every power that scatters God's people, God has a workman ready to break it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns! And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these?" And he said to me, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem." Then the LORD showed me four craftsmen. And I said, "What are these coming to do?" He said, "These are the horns that scattered Judah, so that no one raised his head. And these have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations who lifted up their horns against the land of Judah to scatter it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For every power that has crushed God’s people, God has a workman ready to break it.

Four horns! A horn pictures power, as a bull’s horn is its strength; four stand for power in every direction.

The horns that have scattered Judah. The empires and armies that battered God’s people over centuries. Zechariah does not name them, and we should not press the number into a list of four particular kingdoms. The point is completeness: every power that ever scattered them.

Four craftsmen. For every horn there is a craftsman, a workman with tools, come to cut it down. The number matches exactly. God is never one short.

So that no one raised his head. That is what oppression does: it makes people look at the ground. God’s answer is not a sermon about keeping your chin up. It is workmen.

The lesson of history. Assyria fell to Babylon, Babylon to Persia, and every power that has crushed God’s people has in time been broken. Behind that sequence stands the God who commissions craftsmen. And at the end of the story the last enemy, death itself, is destroyed by Christ, who “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew Bible, 1:18-21 is numbered 2:1-4 (ESV note).

1.title: Return to Me, and I Will Return to You
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the opening of Zechariah’s book, given in the autumn of 520 BC, two months after Haggai began to preach and while the rebuilt temple was barely under way (see the introduction).

The message. God has come back to his people, and he calls them to come back to him. He is not indifferent to his small, struggling people or blind to the comfortable empires around them: he is jealous for Jerusalem, angry with the nations that made her suffering worse, and has returned to her with mercy. Every power that has scattered his people has met, or will meet, its match.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were few, poor and discouraged, with a ruined city, a half-built temple and no sign that God’s great promises were coming true, while Persia was at peace and secure (see the introduction). They needed both a warning not to repeat their fathers’ unbelief and the assurance that heaven had not forgotten them.

How the chapter makes its case. First the call: God’s anger at the fathers was real, and his word overtook them, so this generation must return to him, and he will return to them (vv. 1–6). Then the first vision: horsemen among the myrtles report that the whole earth is at rest, the angel of the LORD asks “how long?”, and God answers with comfort: he is jealous for Zion, angry with the nations at ease, and will rebuild his house and his cities (vv. 7–17). The second vision shows four horns, the powers that scattered God’s people, and four craftsmen sent to cast them down (vv. 18–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by promise. The God who says “I will return to you” came back in person, and the angel of the LORD, sent by the LORD yet speaking as the LORD, this commentary takes to be the Son before his incarnation, already interceding for Jerusalem as he “always lives to make intercession” for his people now (Hebrews 7:25). And the craftsmen who break the horns point to the one who “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).

For us. No one has to clean themselves up before coming back to God: he says “Return to me”, and he comes. When the world seems comfortable and the church small and tired, he is neither asleep nor uninformed, and his answer to our long “how long?” is gracious and comforting words. Every power that bows God’s people to the ground will in the end be broken.
1.theology:
The initiative in returning is God's: he calls his people back and promises to come to them himself (v. 3; Mal 3:7; Jas 4:8). Each generation must answer for itself, and his word outlives every generation, overtaking those who ignore it (vv. 4-6).

Nothing in the world is hidden from him. He knows when the nations are at ease and his people are not, he keeps his own calendar exactly (v. 12; Jer 29:10), and he answers a long "how long?" with gracious and comforting words (v. 13). He is jealous for his people with a husband's protectiveness, and being his instrument of discipline excuses no one's cruelty (vv. 14-15). For every power that scatters his people, he has a craftsman ready to break it (vv. 20-21).
1.examples: Zechariah preached alongside Haggai: Zechariah the prophet of visions, Haggai the prophet of scaffolding, and the discouraged builders needed both. His first vision has horsemen reporting that the whole world is quiet, which is exactly the problem, and a "how long?" prayed in heaven itself. The chapter ends with a measuring line stretched over a ruined city and four horns met by exactly four workmen with tools.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore say to them, Thus declares the LORD of hosts: Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts.
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the tone for the whole book. God’s first word to a generation that has inherited judgment is an invitation, and the visions that follow show that he has already returned to Jerusalem with mercy (v. 16). It is the same welcome the gospel gives: come as you are, and find that God has come to you first in his Son.

1.reflection:
God says, “Return to me, … and I will return to you” (v. 3), before the people have done anything to repair the damage. Why do we so often feel we must clean ourselves up before coming back to God, and what does this verse say to that instinct?

“Do not be like your fathers” (v. 4). What patterns, good or bad, have you inherited from your family or your church background, and what would it look like to believe God’s word now rather than learn the hard way?

The patrol reports that “all the earth remains at rest” while Jerusalem lies in ruins (v. 11), and the angel of the LORD asks, “how long?” (v. 12). Where does God seem silent to you or to Christians you know, and how does it help that this prayer is prayed in heaven and answered with “gracious and comforting words”?

The four craftsmen match the four horns exactly (vv. 18–21). What powers or pressures keep you or your church looking at the ground (“no one raised his head”, v. 21), and how does this vision, and Christ’s reign over every enemy, change the way you face them?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s plans for his people are bigger than any wall, and he himself will be their protection. A young man goes out with a measuring line to work out the size of Jerusalem’s walls (vv. 1–2). An angel is sent running to stop him: Jerusalem will be like open villages, because so many people and animals will fill it that no wall could hold them (vv. 3–4). That would leave the city defenceless, but God promises to be “a wall of fire all around” her and “the glory in her midst” (v. 5). The surveyor plans for what he can manage; God plans for what he means to give.
verseByVerse.theology: God's plans for his people are larger than their plans, and his protection is better than their walls.

verseByVerse.quote: And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a man with a measuring line in his hand! Then I said, "Where are you going?" And he said to me, "To measure Jerusalem, to see what is its width and what is its length." And behold, the angel who talked with me came forward, and another angel came forward to meet him and said to him, "Run, say to that young man, 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it. And I will be to her a wall of fire all around, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory in her midst.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stops a man measuring Jerusalem for walls, because the city will overflow any wall, and God himself will be its wall of fire and its glory.

A man with a measuring line. (In the Hebrew Bible this chapter begins at 2:5, as the ESV notes.) A sensible man does a sensible thing. Jerusalem’s walls lay in rubble, and would not rise again until Nehemiah’s day, some seventy-five years later (Nehemiah 6:15), so he sets out to measure for them. An angel is sent running to stop him: the surveyor is thinking about a wall, God about a crowd too large for any wall. We measure what we can manage; God plans for what he intends to give.

A wall of fire all around. But a city without walls is defenceless. God’s answer is himself, recalling the pillar of fire and cloud that stood between Israel and Egypt’s army (Exodus 14:19–20).

I will be the glory in her midst. The glory that had left the old temple before the city fell (Ezekiel 10:18–19) will return: God himself at the centre of his people. Here is the church’s security in any age, God around us and God among us, and a congregation with no buildings, money or influence still has both.

The wall we can see. The surveyor’s instinct is ours. We like security we can measure: the savings figure, the insurance policy, the gated street, the five-year plan. None is wrong, and Nehemiah was right to build a wall. But we trust them more than they deserve, because they are under our control, one of the deepest idols of the modern heart. A wall of fire is harder to trust than stone: you cannot inspect it or keep it in a drawer. And the walls we build usually keep out two things: the dangers we fear, and the people we did not plan for.

The city that overflows. The church Christ is building has spilled over every boundary drawn round it since Pentecost. Its safety is not in its walls but in its Lord, who said that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). And the vision is completed in the new Jerusalem, whose gates are never shut and whose light is the glory of God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:23–25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — The Apple of His Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls his scattered people home and warns that whoever harms them harms what is most precious to him. “Up! Up!” he calls to the Jews still settled in Babylon: leave the comfortable land of exile and come back to Zion (vv. 6–7). He has sent his messenger against the nations that plundered them, for “he who touches you touches the apple of his eye” (v. 8). With a wave of his hand the plunderers will become plunder for their former slaves, and then God’s people will know that the LORD of hosts has sent the one who speaks (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: To touch God's people is to touch the most sensitive part of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Up! Up! Flee from the land of the north, declares the LORD. For I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heavens, declares the LORD. Up! Escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus said the LORD of hosts, after his glory sent me to the nations who plundered you, for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye: "Behold, I will shake my hand over them, and they shall become plunder for those who served them. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the exiles still in Babylon to come home, and warns the nations that whoever harms his people harms the apple of his eye.

Flee from the land of the north. Babylon lay east, but armies and travellers reached Judah from the north, round the Fertile Crescent. Many Jews had stayed there, settled and comfortable, while Jerusalem was a building site. God’s call is urgent: come home.

Called out of comfort. God’s people can grow so comfortable in exile that they must be called out of it, and the call does not come from a distant taskmaster: the God who has “returned to Jerusalem with mercy” (1:16) is calling his people to where he is at work.

The apple of his eye. The pupil, the most sensitive and fiercely protected part of the body: touch someone’s eye and the whole body reacts. Moses used the picture of God’s care for Israel in the desert (Deuteronomy 32:10), and David prayed it: “Keep me as the apple of your eye” (Psalm 17:8).

He who touches you. To harm God’s people is to strike at God’s eye. The risen Jesus said the same to a man persecuting the church: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Christ so identifies with his people that what is done to them is done to him.

They shall become plunder. The plunderers become the plunder, and the slaves take the spoil.

Who speaks in “the LORD of hosts has sent me”? The angel of the LORD, who is sent by the LORD and yet speaks as the LORD (vv. 10–11): one of the Old Testament’s clearest hints of the Son sent by the Father. Some think the prophet is speaking, but this speaker shakes his hand over the nations (v. 9), which is God’s own work.

What it does not mean. This verse is sometimes used to say a modern nation must be supported whatever it does. God’s care is for his covenant people, in Christ one people of Jew and Gentile, and it puts no state beyond his justice. Christians should love the Jewish people, pray for their salvation, and judge every nation by God’s standards.

Uncertain wording. “After his glory sent me” is among the book’s most obscure phrases, literally “after glory he sent me” (ESV note). It may mean sent to win glory for God, sent after God’s glory had appeared, or sent with glory. The likely sense: a mission to vindicate God’s honour against the nations that plundered his people. The word for “apple” is also rare, but its sense, the pupil, is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — I Will Dwell in Your Midst
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is coming to live among his people, and his people will include the nations. Zion is told to sing and rejoice, for the LORD says, “I come and I will dwell in your midst” (v. 10). Many nations will join themselves to him and become his people, and the LORD who sends the speaker will claim Judah as his own portion and choose Jerusalem again (vv. 11–12). Then the whole world is told to fall silent, because God has roused himself from his holy dwelling and is on the move (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to a small, frightened community is that he is coming to live among them, and to gather the nations with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst, declares the LORD. And many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people. And I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And the LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land, and will again choose Jerusalem." Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is coming to live among his people, many nations will join them, and the whole world must fall silent before him.

I will dwell in your midst. The summit of the vision: not protection from a distance, but the language of pitching a tent among them, as in the tabernacle. A small community with a half-built temple is told that God means to come and live with them.

Fulfilled in Christ. John opens his Gospel with exactly this promise fulfilled: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The Bible ends with it complete: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD. “My people”, once Israel’s name alone, is given to the nations, a great multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9). That is the gospel announced in advance, and every Gentile Christian is part of the fulfilment.

Judah as his portion. God will take Judah as his own portion, the word used for an inheritance. His people are his treasure, not merely his responsibility.

Be silent, all flesh. The chapter ends with a hush, the command Habakkuk and Zephaniah also gave (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7). All the noisy powers of the world have nothing to say, because “he has roused himself from his holy dwelling”. To a people who wondered whether heaven was asleep while “all the earth remains at rest” (1:11), this is the answer: he is awake and moving, and the right response is awed silence.

Where Christians differ. Dispensational readers expect a literal fulfilment in a future earthly Jerusalem. Much of the Reformed tradition reads these promises as fulfilled in Christ dwelling among us and the nations gathered with believing Israel into one people, completed in the new Jerusalem.

This commentary’s view. The second, because the New Testament applies this very language to Christ, the church and the new creation (John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3). Both agree that God will live with his people and the nations will worship him.

2.title: A Wall of Fire All Around
2.overview:
Where we are. This is the third of Zechariah’s eight night visions, seen on the same night as the horsemen and the horns (1:7–21). Chapter 1 ended with God’s promise that “the measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem” (1:16); now a young man sets out with that line.

The message. God’s plans for his people are bigger than their walls and safer than any wall could make them. Jerusalem will overflow with people, and God himself will be a wall of fire around her and the glory within her. So the scattered must come home, the nations that harmed God’s people will answer to him, and Zion can sing, because God is coming to live among his people, and many nations will join them.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were a few thousand people in a city without walls, surrounded by hostile neighbours, while many of their countrymen stayed comfortably in Babylon (see the introduction). They measured their future by what they could see and build.

How the chapter makes its case. First the vision: a man goes to measure Jerusalem and is stopped, because the city will spill over any wall, and God will be her wall of fire and her glory (vv. 1–5). Then the call to the exiles still in Babylon to flee home, with God’s warning that whoever touches his people touches the apple of his eye (vv. 6–9). Finally the song: God is coming to dwell in Zion’s midst, many nations will become his people, and all flesh must fall silent, because he has roused himself (vv. 10–13).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise. “I will dwell in your midst” is fulfilled when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and the nations joining the LORD are the Gentiles gathered by the gospel into one people with believing Israel. The one who speaks, sent by the LORD yet speaking as the LORD (vv. 9–11), is the Son, sent by the Father. And the city without walls, with God as its light, is completed in the new Jerusalem, where “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. We tend to trust the walls we can measure and control. God offers something better: himself around us and among us, and a family wider than any wall we would draw. Those who belong to Christ are as precious to God as the pupil of his eye, and they can live without fear and with doors open to the nations.
2.theology:
God's plans for his people are larger than the plans they make for themselves, and he himself is their security and their glory, which is better than any wall (vv. 2-5). He calls them out of comfortable exile to where he is working (vv. 6-7), and whoever harms them touches the most sensitive part of God (v. 8; Deut 32:10; Ps 17:8; Acts 9:4).

His great promise is not distance but presence: he comes to dwell among his people, fulfilled in Christ and completed in the new creation (v. 10; John 1:14; Rev 21:3), with many nations joined to him and called "my people" (v. 11). When he rouses himself to act, all flesh is to be silent (v. 13).
2.examples: The chapter opens with a surveyor measuring for walls, stopped by an angel at a run, because God means the city to outgrow every boundary anyone could draw, with a ring of fire for its wall. It closes with exiles too comfortable in Babylon to come home, God’s promise to come and live among people who had only a half-built temple, and the whole world told to be quiet because God has stood up.

keyVerse.quote: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The whole vision builds to this promise. The wall of fire and the glory within (v. 5) are finally God’s own presence among his people, and that is why the city can live without walls and welcome the nations. It was fulfilled when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and it will be complete when God makes his home with his people for ever.

2.reflection:
The young man sets out to measure Jerusalem for walls and is stopped, because God plans a city too full for walls (vv. 1–4). Where do you or your church tend to plan by what you can measure and control, and what would it look like to plan by what God intends to give?

God promises to be “a wall of fire all around” and “the glory in her midst” (v. 5). Which do you find harder to trust, God around you as protection or God among you as your glory, and why?

Many exiles had grown comfortable in Babylon and had to be called home (vv. 6–7). In what ways can Christians grow comfortable in a world that is not their home, and what helps us hear God’s call to where he is at work?

“Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people” (v. 11). How does this promise, fulfilled in Christ, shape the way your church welcomes people unlike its current members?

The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?"<sup>3</sup>Now Joshua was standing before the angel, clothed with filthy garments.<sup>4</sup>And the angel said to those who were standing before him, "Remove the filthy garments from him." And to him he said, "Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments."<sup>5</sup>And I said, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." So they put a clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD was standing by.<sup>6</sup>And the angel of the LORD solemnly assured Joshua,<sup>7</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: If you will walk in my ways and keep my charge, then you shall rule my house and have charge of my courts, and I will give you the right of access among those who are standing here.<sup>8</sup>Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign: behold, I will bring my servant the Branch.<sup>9</sup>For behold, on the stone that I have set before Joshua, on a single stone with seven eyes, I will engrave its inscription, declares the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.<sup>10</sup>In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, every one of you will invite his neighbor to come under his vine and under his fig tree."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the accuser not by denying the charges but by taking away the guilt. Joshua the high priest, standing for the whole people, appears before the angel of the LORD, and Satan stands beside him to accuse him (v. 1). The LORD rebukes Satan on the ground of his own choice of Jerusalem: Joshua is a brand snatched from the fire (v. 2). Yet Joshua’s clothes really are filthy (v. 3). So the angel orders them removed, declares his iniquity taken away and clothes him in pure garments; Zechariah asks for a clean turban too, and it is done (vv. 4–5). Grace does not overlook sin; it removes it.
verseByVerse.theology: God answers the accusation against his people not by denying the filth but by removing it and clothing them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. And the LORD said to Satan, "The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?" Now Joshua was standing before the angel, clothed with filthy garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan accuses the high priest, who stands for the whole people in filthy clothes, but God silences the accuser because he has chosen and rescued them.

Joshua the high priest. The fourth vision is a courtroom. Joshua the high priest is a real man, working alongside Zerubbabel on the temple (Haggai 1:1). He is the people’s representative before God: when he stands there, they stand there.

Satan standing at his right hand. The prosecutor stands where an accuser stood in court. The name means “the Accuser” or “the Adversary” (ESV note), and Revelation calls him “the accuser of our brothers … who accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10).

True accusations. The charges were not false. The priesthood had failed, the nation had earned its exile, and Joshua had nothing to say. Satan’s charges against Christians are often true too, which is what makes them so effective.

The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! God does not answer the accusation with an argument; he silences the accuser. And the ground of the rebuke is not Joshua’s record but God’s choice: “The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem.” Notice too who speaks. Joshua stands before the angel of the LORD (v. 1), and “the LORD” rebukes Satan in the name of the LORD: the angel speaks as God and appeals to God, a glimpse of the Son who is both our judge and our advocate (1 John 2:1). Jude recalls the same words on the lips of the archangel Michael: “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9).

A brand plucked from the fire. A brand is a burning stick (ESV note): Joshua is half-burnt wood snatched from the flames of exile. He is not impressive; he is rescued, and rescued things belong to their rescuer.

Every accusation answered. Here is the answer to every accusation a believer will face. Not “I am better than you say”, but “God has pulled me out of the fire, and he is the one you are arguing with”. Paul puts it as a question and its answer: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

Clothed with filthy garments. The Bible does not tidy up the picture. The word is a strong one: clothes soiled in the most disgusting way. That is how sin looks in heaven’s light, and dressing it up helps nobody. For the first hearers it was alarming. The high priest’s garments were made “for glory and for beauty” (Exodus 28:2), and he served on behalf of everyone; if he stood before God defiled, so did every sacrifice the rebuilt temple would offer.
verseByVerse.note: Joshua the high priest stands before God for the whole people, and the accuser's charges against him are charges against them all.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to those who were standing before him, "Remove the filthy garments from him." And to him he said, "Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments." And I said, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." So they put a clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD was standing by.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God strips away the high priest’s filthy clothes, takes his guilt away and dresses him in clean garments: the gospel in a picture.

Remove the filthy garments. Watch the order, because it is the gospel. First, God acts. Joshua does not wash his clothes, promise to do better or defend himself; he is stripped by others while he stands there.

I have taken your iniquity away from you. Second, God explains. Where the iniquity went is not said here; the New Testament tells us it was laid on Christ, who dealt with it “by canceling the record of debt that stood against us … nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14).

I will clothe you with pure vestments. Third, God clothes. He does not leave his people standing naked once the filth is gone. Isaiah sings of it: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). In Revelation the saints wear robes washed “in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14).

A better high priest. Joshua could only stand there and be cleansed. The high priest Christians trust needed no cleansing: he is “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26). Yet he took our filth as his own: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The exchange in this vision, filth off and clean robes on, is the exchange made at the cross. (Joshua is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus.)

Let them put a clean turban on his head. Zechariah, watching, cannot keep quiet. The high priest’s turban carried a golden plate engraved “Holy to the LORD” (Exodus 28:36–38). He wants the man fully restored, not merely cleaned up, and a spectator’s prayer is answered in the middle of a vision. It is a good instinct for believers watching someone else’s restoration: ask for the turban too, full reinstatement rather than grudging tolerance.

Can’t I just tell myself I am enough? That is our culture’s advice about the accusing voice inside. It is kindly meant, and some of those voices are cruel lies that deserve silencing. But many accusations are true, and we know it: Joshua’s garments really were filthy. Telling a guilty conscience it is imagining things does not quiet it for long; it goes underground and comes out as anxiety, defensiveness or a constant need for reassurance. No one can acquit himself in a court where he is the defendant. Joshua receives something better: someone with authority over the court speaks for him, takes the filth away and dresses him. The Christian does not say, “I am enough.” He says that Christ is enough for him, and that is the only verdict that survives a long look in the mirror.

Uncertain wording. The word for “turban” is not the usual one for the high priest’s headdress; elsewhere it is used of other turbans (Job 29:14; Isaiah 3:23) and once of a royal diadem (Isaiah 62:3). It may be a simple variation, or a hint of the priest who will also be king (6:11–13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cleansed priest is given a calling, and his cleansing becomes a sign of a far greater cleansing to come. Joshua is charged to walk in God’s ways and keep his service, with the promise of rule in God’s house and access among those who stand in his presence (vv. 6–7). Then he and his fellow priests are told that they are a sign: God will bring his servant the Branch, the promised son of David (v. 8). On a stone set before Joshua God will engrave an inscription and remove the iniquity of the land in a single day (v. 9). The result will be peace, neighbours inviting one another under vine and fig tree (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The cleansing of one priest points to the coming of the Branch, who takes away a nation's guilt in a single day.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD solemnly assured Joshua, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: If you will walk in my ways and keep my charge, then you shall rule my house and have charge of my courts, and I will give you the right of access among those who are standing here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cleansed priest is called to walk in God’s ways, and promised real responsibility and a place in God’s own presence.

If you will walk in my ways. After the grace comes the charge: Joshua is cleansed first and commanded second. The “if” does not make his forgiveness conditional; it describes how he is to serve. So it is for Christians: we walk in God’s ways as people already clothed by him, and the Spirit he has given causes us to walk in them (Ezekiel 36:27).

You shall rule my house. Three things are promised: real responsibility (“rule my house”), real authority (“have charge of my courts”), and best of all, “the right of access among those who are standing here”, that is, among the angels in God’s presence.

The right of access. The high priest entered the Most Holy Place, God’s presence, once a year on the Day of Atonement, with blood and with fear; this promises something freer. Christians have it in full: through Christ we have “access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18), and may draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign: behold, I will bring my servant the Branch. For behold, on the stone that I have set before Joshua, on a single stone with seven eyes, I will engrave its inscription, declares the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day. In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, every one of you will invite his neighbor to come under his vine and under his fig tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cleansed priests are a sign that God will send his servant the Branch and remove his people’s guilt in a single day, bringing peace.

Men who are a sign. Joshua and his fellow priests point beyond themselves: you have been cleansed, and one is coming who will do this for everyone.

My servant the Branch. “My servant” is Isaiah’s title for the one who would bear his people’s iniquities (Isaiah 53:11). “The Branch” is the promised king from David’s fallen family tree: “I will raise up for David a righteous Branch” (Jeremiah 23:5), “a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1). Zechariah will use the title again and add something remarkable: this Branch will be both priest and king on one throne (6:12–13).

In a single day. Whatever the stone means, the last clause is unmistakable: “I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.” Not gradually, not by a lifetime of sacrifices, but in one day. The Day of Atonement came round every year, because it never finished the job.

Which day this was. Christians know. “We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”, and “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:10, 14). What was promised to a man in filthy clothes was accomplished on a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem.

Under his vine and under his fig tree. The result of forgiveness is neighbourliness: Micah’s picture of peace, each under his own vine and fig tree (Micah 4:4). People who know their own filthy garments have been taken away are not hard to live next door to, and that is a fine test of whether grace has taken hold.

Where Christians differ. Many scholars think the Branch first meant Zerubbabel, David’s descendant then governing Judah. Christians have generally read it as the Messiah, with Zerubbabel at most a pointer to him.

This commentary’s view. The Branch is the Messiah, Jesus: God speaks of him as still to come, and in 6:12–13 he unites priest and king, which no governor of Judah ever did.

Uncertain wording. The “stone” may be a foundation stone of the temple or a jewel on the high priest’s clothing, perhaps the gold plate on his turban. The “seven eyes” may mean “facets” (ESV note), or picture God’s complete sight (compare 4:10). The inscription is not given. We should not claim more certainty than the text gives; the clear point is the promise that follows.
verseByVerse.note: “The Branch” is a title of the coming Messiah.

3.title: Filthy Garments and Clean Vestments
3.overview:
Where we are. This is the fourth of Zechariah’s eight night visions, at the centre of the series with chapter 4. The first three promised that God would rebuild his city and dwell in it (1:7–2:13); but a holy God cannot live among an unclean people led by an unclean priest.

The message. God himself takes away his people’s guilt. Joshua the high priest stands before God in filthy clothes with Satan accusing him, and he has nothing to say; but the LORD rebukes the accuser, strips off the filth and clothes him in clean garments. And this cleansing of one priest is a sign of something greater: God will send his servant the Branch and remove the iniquity of the land in a single day.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were rebuilding a temple, but its people and priest were stained by the sins that had brought the exile (see the introduction). Would God accept their worship at all, or did the accuser have the last word?

How the chapter makes its case. First the accusation and the rebuke: Satan stands to accuse Joshua, but the LORD, who has chosen Jerusalem, silences him, for Joshua is a brand plucked from the fire (vv. 1–3). Then the exchange: the filthy garments are removed, his iniquity is taken away, and he is clothed in pure vestments and a clean turban (vv. 4–5). Then the charge: cleansed, Joshua is to walk in God’s ways, with the promise of access to God’s presence (vv. 6–7). Finally the sign: Joshua and his fellow priests point to the coming Branch, and to a single day when the land’s iniquity will be removed, bringing peace under vine and fig tree (vv. 8–10).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise and by pattern. “My servant the Branch” is the promised Messiah, David’s descendant, whom Zechariah will later show as priest and king at once (6:12–13). The single day on which iniquity is removed is the day of the cross, when Christ by “a single offering … has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). And Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, is a pattern of the greater high priest, who needed no cleansing but took our filth so that we could wear his righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21).

For us. When the accuser points to our sins, we need not argue our case or pretend we are clean. Our defence is not our record but God’s choice and Christ’s sacrifice: he takes the filthy garments away and clothes us himself. And people forgiven like that become easy neighbours.
3.theology:
Satan accuses God's people, and his charges are often true (v. 1; Rev 12:10). God silences him not by argument but by his own choice and rescue of his people (v. 2; Rom 8:33-34), and he deals with sin rather than dressing it up.

The order of grace is that God removes the filth, takes away the iniquity and clothes his people himself (v. 4; Isa 61:10; Rev 7:14; Col 2:14); the charge to serve, and the great privilege of access to his presence, come after (vv. 6-7). The cleansing of one priest is a sign of the Branch, the promised servant-king (v. 8; Isa 11:1; Jer 23:5), who removed iniquity in a single day at the cross (v. 9; Heb 10:10, 14).
3.examples: The vision is a courtroom in which every accusation is true, and a high priest stands before God in disgusting clothes, a half-burnt stick pulled out of a fire. Someone else strips the filth off a man who cannot do it himself, and a bystander asks for the turban as well and gets it. It ends with a Day of Atonement that never has to be repeated, and forgiven neighbours inviting each other under the fig tree.

keyVerse.quote: And the angel said to those who were standing before him, “Remove the filthy garments from him.” And to him he said, “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments.”
keyVerse.note: This verse is the gospel in a picture. The guilty priest does nothing but stand there: God removes the filth, declares the iniquity taken away and clothes him in clean garments. It is the exchange Christ made at the cross, our sin laid on him and his righteousness given to us.

3.reflection:
Satan’s accusations against Joshua were true, yet the LORD rebuked him (vv. 1–3). How does the accuser use true charges against Christians, and what is the difference between hearing his voice and hearing the Holy Spirit’s conviction of sin?

Joshua does nothing to clean himself: others remove his garments and clothe him (vv. 4–5). Why do we find it so hard to receive forgiveness this way, and how does Christ’s exchange at the cross (2 Corinthians 5:21) answer the advice to “tell yourself you are enough”?

Zechariah asks for a clean turban, full restoration rather than mere cleaning (v. 5). When someone in your church has fallen and repented, what does it look like to ask for “the turban too”?

The chapter ends with forgiven people inviting their neighbours under vine and fig tree (v. 10). How should knowing that our guilt has been removed in “a single day” change the way we treat the people around us this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Lampstand and the Word to Zerubbabel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s work is finished by God’s Spirit, not by human strength, and every obstacle will give way. The angel wakes Zechariah to see a golden lampstand with a bowl and seven lamps, with two olive trees beside it (vv. 1–3). Zechariah asks what it means and admits he does not know (vv. 4–5). The answer is a word for Zerubbabel the governor: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (v. 6). The great mountain in his way will become a plain, and he will bring out the top stone to shouts of “Grace, grace to it!” (v. 7). The lamp burns because the oil never stops.
verseByVerse.theology: God's work is done by his Spirit, not by human resources, and the finished result is all of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel who talked with me came again and woke me, like a man who is awakened out of his sleep. And he said to me, "What do you see?" I said, "I see, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, with a bowl on the top of it, and seven lamps on it, with seven lips on each of the lamps that are on the top of it. And there are two olive trees by it, one on the right of the bowl and the other on its left." And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?" Then the angel who talked with me answered and said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah sees a golden lampstand kept burning by two living olive trees: light from a supply no human hand provides.

Like a man who is awakened out of his sleep. Even a prophet gets tired, and God works round the frailty of his messengers.

A lampstand all of gold. Like the temple lampstand, with a difference: a bowl of oil on top and two living olive trees feeding it. The old lampstand needed priests to carry in oil every day (Leviticus 24:2–4); this one is supplied continuously, without human effort.

Do you not know what these are? Zechariah answers, “No, my lord”, and it is a healthy instinct: he does not invent a meaning. Much confusion in Bible reading comes from refusing to admit we do not know.

Uncertain wording. “Seven lips on each of the lamps” is compressed in Hebrew. It may mean seven spouts for wicks on each lamp, forty-nine flames in all, or seven spouts in total. Either way: abundant light from one supply.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts. Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain. And he shall bring forward the top stone amid shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple will be finished by God’s Spirit, not by human strength, every obstacle will be levelled, and the work will end in praise of God’s grace.

Not by might, nor by power. Think who first heard it. Zerubbabel governed a province with no army, treasury or political weight, while neighbouring officials challenged the work and reported it to the Persian court (Ezra 5:3–17). Might and power were exactly what he did not have.

But by my Spirit. God does not promise him might and power, but his Spirit. The lampstand burns because the oil never stops flowing, not because anyone is running to fill it.

What it does not mean. Not a warning against effort: Zerubbabel’s own hands will finish the house (v. 9). It says what actually makes the work go. Churches are tempted to think they need more resources, better methods or stronger personalities; those may help, but they are not the power. The temple was finished by the Spirit through ordinary hands, and the church grows the same way, by the Spirit Christ poured out (Acts 1:8).

Who are you, O great mountain? The obstacle is addressed to its face. Opposition, poverty or discouragement, it will be flattened (compare Matthew 17:20).

Grace, grace to it! The last stone goes up amid shouts not of “well done us” but of grace, because the whole work was a gift from beginning to end.

A greater stone. Christians have also thought here of a greater stone. The psalm sang of “The stone that the builders rejected” which “has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22), and Jesus applied it to himself (Matthew 21:42). Peter writes that God laid in Zion “a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious” (1 Peter 2:6). When the last living stone of God’s true temple is set in place, the shout will be the same: grace, grace to it.

Uncertain wording. “The top stone” may be the capstone that completes the building, or, as some think, a stone from the old temple laid to link the new house with the old. “Grace, grace to it” may be a prayer for God’s favour on the building or a cry of delight at its beauty. Either way, the glory goes to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Day of Small Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Small beginnings in God’s work are not to be despised, because God finishes what he starts and sees everything. The hands of Zerubbabel that laid the foundation will complete the temple, proving that God sent his messenger (vv. 8–9). Those who despised the day of small things will rejoice to see the builder’s tool in his hand, for the seven lamps are the eyes of the LORD ranging through the whole earth (v. 10). Zechariah then asks twice about the olive trees and their branches (vv. 11–13), and learns that they are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth (v. 14): servants through whom God supplies his people, not the source.
verseByVerse.theology: God finishes what he starts, delights in small beginnings, and keeps his servants supplied.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also complete it. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. "These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hands that began the temple will finish it, so no one should despise its small beginnings, for the LORD sees all that is done for him.

His hands shall also complete it. God does not leave things half built. The foundation laid about sixteen years earlier had been abandoned; the same hands will set the last stone, and the temple was completed in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15), though Ezra does not name Zerubbabel at the dedication. Paul says the same of God’s work in a person: he “who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

The day of small things. Some had looked at this temple and sneered, as the old men had wept over it (Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:3). God simply says they will end up rejoicing when they see the plumb line in the governor’s hand, the ordinary tool of a builder checking his wall.

In everyday life. Most of God’s work looks small while it is happening: a handful of people praying, one hard conversation, a child taught patiently. Despising small days usually means we have mistaken size for significance.

Why will small things not fail? The seven lamps are “the eyes of the LORD”, and nothing done for him in a back street is unobserved: “the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (2 Chronicles 16:9).

Uncertain wording. “The plumb line” is literally a stone of tin or metal: probably a plummet for checking a wall, though some think it a metal tablet laid at the finishing. Either way the work is going ahead. “These seven” picks up the seven lamps of verse 2, so verses 6–10 are a word to Zerubbabel set within the vision’s explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to him, "What are these two olive trees on the right and the left of the lampstand?" And a second time I answered and said to him, "What are these two branches of the olive trees, which are beside the two golden pipes from which the golden oil is poured out?" He said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord." Then he said, "These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two olive trees are God’s two anointed servants, through whom he keeps his people supplied, and who point to the one Anointed who is both king and priest.

What are these two branches of the olive trees? Zechariah asks twice: he wants to know where the supply comes from.

The two anointed ones. Most take them to be the two leaders of that community: Zerubbabel the governor, from David’s line, and Joshua the high priest. Through these two men, one royal and one priestly, God kept his people’s lamp alight.

Who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. Servants, not the source. The oil is God’s.

Two offices joined. The two offices were never meant to stay apart. In 6:11–13 a crown is placed on Joshua’s head, with the promise that the Branch “shall be a priest on his throne” (6:13). What took two men in 520 BC is held by one now. Jesus Christ, whose title Christ means “Anointed”, is king and priest together, and his people are kept burning by his Spirit.

Revelation’s lampstands. The churches are lampstands (Revelation 1:20), and the two witnesses are “the two olive trees and the two lampstands” (Revelation 11:4). The church’s calling is not to generate light but to hold it, and to stay connected to the supply.

Where Christians differ. Some identify the two anointed ones as the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, or as heavenly servants.

This commentary’s view. They are Zerubbabel and Joshua: the book joins these two leaders again in 6:9–13, and kings and priests were the ones anointed with oil.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “branches” usually means ears of grain, so it may mean fruit-laden tips or channels for the oil. Verse 12 lacks the word “oil”, reading simply “the golden” (ESV note), probably golden oil. “Anointed ones” is literally “sons of new oil” (ESV note), not the usual phrase for anointing. The picture is clear: God’s oil, through his servants, keeps the light burning.

4.title: Not by Might, nor by Power
4.overview:
Where we are. This is the fifth of Zechariah’s eight night visions, paired with chapter 3 at the centre of the series. There Joshua the high priest was cleansed; here the word is for Zerubbabel the governor, the descendant of David who had laid the temple’s foundation and now had to finish it.

The message. God’s work is done by God’s Spirit, not by human strength, so small and weak beginnings are no reason for despair. The temple will be finished because God supplies what his people lack, as living olive trees keep a lamp burning without anyone filling it. Every mountain in the way will be levelled, the hands that began the work will complete it, and the only fitting shout at the end will be “Grace!”

Why it was said. Zerubbabel governed a tiny province with no army and no money, the foundation had lain abandoned for years, local officials had challenged the work before the Persian court, and some people looked at the modest new building and despised it (see the introduction; Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:3).

How the chapter makes its case. Zechariah is woken to see a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees (vv. 1–5). The explanation comes as a word to Zerubbabel: not by might or power but by God’s Spirit; the great mountain will become a plain, and the top stone will go up to shouts of “Grace, grace to it!” (vv. 6–7). Then a second word: Zerubbabel’s hands will finish what they began, and those who despised the day of small things will rejoice, for the eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth (vv. 8–10). Finally the olive trees are explained as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth (vv. 11–14).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and pattern. The two anointed leaders, a king’s son and a priest, are joined two chapters later in the Branch who “shall be a priest on his throne” (6:13). Jesus is that one Anointed, king and priest together, who builds the true temple of God’s people by his Spirit, the stone the builders rejected that has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22; Matthew 21:42). And the Spirit by whom the temple was finished is the Spirit he poured out at Pentecost.

For us. Churches and Christians often feel small, under-resourced and faced with mountains. This chapter does not tell us to try harder or to despise small beginnings; it tells us where the power lies. Do the ordinary work faithfully, pray for the Spirit, and expect to give God all the credit at the end.
4.theology:
God's work is accomplished by his Spirit rather than by human resources, which does not make human effort unnecessary (vv. 6, 9). Mountains are levelled before his purposes, and he completes what he begins, so that the only fitting shout at the end is about grace (vv. 7, 9).

He does not despise small beginnings, and his eyes range over the whole earth to support his people (v. 10; 2 Chr 16:9). He supplies them through appointed servants who stand by him and are not themselves the source; and the offices of king and priest, held by two men here, are united in Christ (v. 14; 6:13).
4.examples: A tired prophet is woken mid-vision to see a lampstand fed by living trees instead of by servants with jars. A governor with no army is told what his real resource is, a mountain is asked to its face who it thinks it is, and the last stone of a building is greeted with "Grace, grace!" The seven lamps turn out to be the eyes of God, watching the plumb line in the hands that finished what they started.

keyVerse.quote: This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.
keyVerse.note: The whole vision of the lampstand is explained in this sentence. A weak governor with no army or wealth is told that God’s house will be finished by God’s Spirit, just as the lamp burns from oil no one carries in. It is still how God builds his church: through ordinary people, by the Spirit Christ gives, so that the praise is all his.

4.reflection:
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (v. 6). Where are you or your church most tempted to rely on resources, methods or personalities, and what would it look like this week to depend on the Spirit while still doing the work?

Zechariah twice admits, “No, my lord” (vv. 5, 13), rather than invent a meaning. Why is it sometimes hard to admit we do not understand a passage or a situation, and how can a group make it easier to do so?

“Whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice” (v. 10). What small things in your life or church are you tempted to despise, and how does it help to know that “the eyes of the LORD” range through the whole earth?

The two anointed ones point to Jesus, king and priest in one person (v. 14; 6:13). How does knowing that Christ both rules you and represents you before God give you confidence when the mountains in front of you look large?
