verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s law does not stay on the page: it goes out looking for sin, and it finds it at home. Zechariah sees a scroll about thirty feet by fifteen, flying open over the land where no one can miss it (vv. 1–2). It is the curse of God’s covenant, and its two sides name two sins, stealing and swearing falsely by God’s name, which between them stand for wrong done to a neighbour and wrong done to God (v. 3). The LORD himself sends it out, and it does not hover outside: it enters the house of the thief and the perjurer, settles there and eats the house away, timber and stones (v. 4). Secret sin is not safe sin.
verseByVerse.theology: God's law is not a document filed away but a living word that goes out and searches houses.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a flying scroll! And he said to me, "What do you see?" I answered, "I see a flying scroll. Its length is twenty cubits, and its width ten cubits." Then he said to me, "This is the curse that goes out over the face of the whole land. For everyone who steals shall be cleaned out according to what is on one side, and everyone who swears falsely shall be cleaned out according to what is on the other side. I will send it out, declares the LORD of hosts, and it shall enter the house of the thief, and the house of him who swears falsely by my name. And it shall remain in his house and consume it, both timber and stones."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s law goes out over the whole land and enters the homes of those who wrong their neighbour or God, to destroy them from within. No sin is too private for God’s word to find.

A flying scroll! The sixth vision is strange even by Zechariah’s standards: an enormous scroll, open and airborne. A cubit was about 18 inches, so it is roughly thirty feet by fifteen. It sails over the country where everyone can read it: God’s word is public and impossible to ignore.

Both halves of the law. Each side of the scroll names a sin: stealing, which wrongs a neighbour, and swearing falsely by God’s name, which wrongs God (Leviticus 19:12). Between them they cover both halves of the ten commandments. The community rebuilding the temple was still cheating one another and using God’s name carelessly (8:16–17), which is why these two appear.

It shall enter the house of the thief. The LORD of hosts sends the scroll, and it does not stay in the street. It enters the house, where nobody sees, and stays to “consume it, both timber and stones”. That is how secret sin works on a home: not usually dramatically, it quietly eats the beams and the walls until one day the structure gives way.

Christ and the curse. None of us has kept these two commands perfectly, and the only safety is to have the curse dealt with. Christ “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). So when that scroll has entered our house, the answer is not to hide the sin in the walls but to confess it to the God who forgives (Psalm 32:5), and then, by his Spirit, to give back what was taken and speak the truth.

What it does not mean. Not that every family trouble is punishment for a hidden sin (John 9:2–3). The vision warns the guilty; it does not diagnose other people’s misfortunes.

Uncertain wording. Verse 3 is compressed. The verb rendered “shall be cleaned out” usually means to go unpunished, so some read a complaint (thieves have gone unpunished until now) which the scroll ends. “According to what is on one side” probably means by what is written on that side. The ESV notes that “falsely” is supplied from verse 4. On every reading the sinner will not escape.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty cubits by ten were also the measurements of the porch of Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 6:3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God does more than restrain his people’s sin: he removes it from among them and sends it where it belongs. A grain basket goes out, and the angel says it is the iniquity of the whole land (vv. 5–6). Under its lead lid sits a woman, Wickedness, alive and trying to get out, and she is thrust back and sealed in (vv. 7–8). Two women with wings like a stork’s carry the basket off between earth and heaven (v. 9), to the land of Shinar, the plain of Babel, where a house will be built for it (vv. 10–11). Sin is deported to the city of pride, and the land is left clean for the God who has come to live in it.
verseByVerse.theology: God does not merely forgive his people's sin; he removes it from among them and sends it where it belongs.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel who talked with me came forward and said to me, "Lift your eyes and see what this is that is going out." And I said, "What is it?" He said, "This is the basket that is going out." And he said, "This is their iniquity in all the land." And behold, the leaden cover was lifted, and there was a woman sitting in the basket! And he said, "This is Wickedness." And he thrust her back into the basket, and thrust down the leaden weight on its opening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sin of the whole land is gathered into a grain basket, and inside it Wickedness is alive and trying to get out, until she is forced back under a lid of lead.

The basket that is going out. The seventh vision follows. The “basket” is literally an ephah, a grain measure of about 22 litres (the ESV notes), the everyday container of buying and selling: a fit symbol for the sin of a trading community, with its short measures and false weights. “This is their iniquity in all the land”: the sins of the scroll gathered into a single load.

This is Wickedness. Inside the basket Wickedness is alive, sitting in the middle of ordinary commerce, and she wants out: she has to be thrust back and the lead weight thrust down on the opening. Left to itself, evil comes up and out. Yet the angel deals with her in a moment: wickedness is real and restless, but it is not stronger than God.

Why a woman? Because the Hebrew word for wickedness is feminine. It says nothing about women, any more than the picture of Wisdom as a woman in Proverbs means that women are wiser than men.

Textual note. Where the ESV has “iniquity” (v. 6), the standard Hebrew text reads “eye”, probably meaning appearance; the ESV follows one Hebrew manuscript and the Greek Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, two women coming forward! The wind was in their wings. They had wings like the wings of a stork, and they lifted up the basket between earth and heaven. Then I said to the angel who talked with me, "Where are they taking the basket?" He said to me, "To the land of Shinar, to build a house for it. And when this is prepared, they will set the basket down there on its base."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has his people’s sin carried right out of the land to Babylon, the city of pride, where it is given a house: he does not only forgive their sin, he removes it from among them.

Two women coming forward! Two winged figures arrive, with wings like a stork’s and the wind behind them. They lift the basket “between earth and heaven” and carry it away. We should not force the details: the point is that the sin of the land is being removed, thoroughly, by a power the people had nothing to do with.

To the land of Shinar. The old name for Babylonia, the plain where Babel was built (Genesis 11:2). Wickedness is deported to Babylon, the Bible’s standing symbol of human pride organised against God, and there it gets a “house” of its own, set on its base like an idol: a temple where it will be worshipped openly. What God removes from his people does not evaporate; it goes to the place that wants it. But that city has its end too (Revelation 18).

Cleansing before crowning. This is the last vision of cleansing before the crowning of Joshua in chapter 6: first the sin is removed, then the priest-king is crowned.

Like the Day of Atonement. On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid the people’s sins on a goat, which was led into the wilderness: it “shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area” (Leviticus 16:22). John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). What the basket pictures, Christ accomplished: sin not only covered but carried away.

A clean people. For the small community in Jerusalem this is pure comfort: God intended a people not merely forgiven but purged. That is what he is doing in his church, and what he will finish on the last day, when “nothing unclean will ever enter” his city (Revelation 21:27).

5.title: The Flying Scroll and the Basket
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 holds the sixth and seventh of Zechariah’s eight night visions (1:7–6:8). Joshua the high priest has been stripped of his filthy garments (chapter 3) and Zerubbabel promised that the Spirit will finish the temple (chapter 4); now God turns to the sin of the people.

The message. God will not live among a people who keep their sin, and he will not leave them to clean themselves up. His word goes out and finds sin where it hides, even inside the house; then he himself lifts the sin out of the land and sends it far away, to the place where it belongs. The holy God who has come back to Jerusalem means to have a clean people.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were building a house for God while still cheating one another and taking his name lightly (compare 7:9–10; 8:16–17; see the introduction). A new temple would not cure that, and these visions show that God intends to deal with it himself.

How the chapter makes its case. First a vast flying scroll, the curse of God’s law on the thief and the false swearer, sweeps over the land and enters their houses to consume them (vv. 1–4): sin will be exposed and judged. Then a grain basket holding a woman called Wickedness is shut under a lid of lead (vv. 5–8), and two winged women carry it off to Shinar, the land of Babylon, where a house is built for it (vv. 9–11): sin will be taken right away from God’s people. Judgment and removal clear the way for the crowning of chapter 6.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by pattern. The scroll’s curse falls on everyone who has stolen or sworn falsely, which in the end means all of us, and the only safe place is under the one who “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The basket carried far away echoes the goat of the Day of Atonement, which bore Israel’s iniquities “to a remote area” (Leviticus 16:22), and both point to “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). The house built for Wickedness in Shinar looks ahead to the fall of Babylon the great (Revelation 18), and to the city into which “nothing unclean will ever enter” (Revelation 21:27).

For us. God’s word still reaches into private rooms, and secret sin still eats at a home from the inside; the way out is not to hide it in the walls but to bring it into the light, to Christ. And believers may take heart: the God who exposes sin is the God who carries it away, and he will not stop until his people are clean.
5.theology:
God's law goes out publicly and searches private houses, and one curse covers sin against a neighbour and sin against God's name alike; secret sin consumes a home from the inside (vv. 3-4). Christ redeemed his people from that curse by becoming a curse for them (Gal 3:13).

Wickedness is not passive and must be held down (v. 8), but God does more than restrain or forgive it: he removes it from his people, and it is enshrined and finally judged in the city built against him (vv. 9-11; Gen 11:2). The cleansing of his people comes before the crowning of their priest-king (6:11-13).
5.examples: A scroll the size of a room flies where everyone can read it, then goes indoors and stays in the walls. A grain basket, the everyday container of a trading people, has something alive inside, held down by a heavy lead lid. Then sin is airlifted out of the country on stork's wings, to a house built for it in Babylon.

keyVerse.quote: And he said, “This is Wickedness.” And he thrust her back into the basket, and thrust down the leaden weight on its opening.
keyVerse.note: This verse names what the whole chapter is about. Wickedness is alive and restless, and it wants out, but it is not stronger than God: his angel shuts it in, and in the next verses he has it carried far away. Holiness for God’s people begins not with their effort but with his work of dealing with sin, done fully when Christ bore the curse and took away the sin of the world.

5.reflection:
The flying scroll enters the house to “consume it, both timber and stones” (v. 4). How have you seen hidden sin, such as dishonesty or careless words, quietly damage a home, a friendship or a church? Why is concealing it so tempting, and what does Psalm 32:5 offer instead?

The scroll names one sin against a neighbour and one against God (v. 3). Why do the two belong together? Where in daily life is it easiest to be careless with money that is not ours, or with God’s name?

Wickedness has to be thrust back and held down under a lead weight (vv. 7–8). What does that picture teach about the nature of sin, and about why we cannot deal with it in our own strength?

God does not only forgive sin; he carries it away (vv. 9–11). How do the Day of Atonement and John’s words “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29) help you believe that about your own sin?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The powers that move through world history go out only at God’s command, and they do not rest until his justice is done. The last night vision answers the first: where horsemen once reported a world at ease (1:11), now four chariots come out from between two bronze mountains, drawn by red, black, white and dappled horses (vv. 1–3). They go out to the four winds of heaven, but only after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth (vv. 4–5). Straining to be gone, they are released to patrol the earth (vv. 6–7), and word comes back that those who went north, towards Babylon, have set God’s Spirit at rest there (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's patrols go out from his presence to every direction, and his purposes are at rest only when justice is done.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots came out from between two mountains. And the mountains were mountains of bronze. The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses, the third white horses, and the fourth chariot dappled horses—all of them strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last vision answers the first: where horsemen once reported a world at ease (1:11), God now sends chariots, which are for war, from his own presence to every corner of the earth.

The mountains were mountains of bronze. Two mountains of bronze suggest a fixed, immovable place: the gateway of God’s throne room, from which his decisions issue.

The four colours. Revelation’s four horsemen draw on this imagery (Revelation 6:1–8). We are not told what the colours mean, but four is the Bible’s number for the whole world: these teams cover everything, under one command.

Uncertain wording. The colour words are uncertain. “Dappled” may mean spotted or piebald, and the word rendered “strong” at the end of verse 3 (and in v. 7) may itself be a colour, perhaps grey; the ESV notes that verse 3 may read “the fourth chariot strong dappled horses”. Since the vision does not explain the colours, it is wise not to build on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I answered and said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?" And the angel answered and said to me, "These are going out to the four winds of heaven, after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth. The chariot with the black horses goes toward the north country, the white ones go after them, and the dappled ones go toward the south country." When the strong horses came out, they were impatient to go and patrol the earth. And he said, "Go, patrol the earth." So they patrolled the earth. Then he cried to me, "Behold, those who go toward the north country have set my Spirit at rest in the north country."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The forces at work in world history go out only after reporting to the Lord of all the earth, and they press on until his just anger against the oppressor is satisfied.

After presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth. The chariots go out “to the four winds of heaven”, but only after standing before God. The forces at work in world history, whatever they are, report for orders first. That is precisely what a small, vulnerable community needed to know.

They were impatient to go. God’s agents are not reluctant; they strain at the bit while he holds them until the hour comes. We often mistake God’s timing for God’s inactivity.

Have set my Spirit at rest in the north country. The “north country” is Babylon, the direction from which invaders always came and where the exiles had been taken; the south country is probably Egypt, Israel’s other ancient oppressor. When God’s judgment has been carried out in the north, his Spirit is “at rest”: his anger against Babylon is satisfied. God is not restless with anxiety, nor indifferent; his purposes press on until wrongs are dealt with, and then there is rest, as there will be on the last day.

The Lord of all the earth. The risen Christ says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). The powers of history still report to him.

Uncertain wording. The word for “winds” also means “spirits”; the ESV notes the reading “These are the four winds of heaven going out” (v. 5). Verse 6 does not mention the red horses, and some think the white ones went west rather than “after them”. “Set my Spirit at rest” most likely means God’s anger is satisfied (compare Ezekiel 5:13), though some take it that his Spirit now rests on the north, stirring exiles there to come home (Ezra 1:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — A Crown for the Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God crowns a priest as a sign of the coming one who will be king and priest together and will build his temple. Zechariah is to take silver and gold from men newly arrived from Babylon, make a crown and set it on the head of Joshua the high priest (vv. 9–11), a startling act in a nation that kept priest and king strictly apart. The word that goes with it looks far beyond Joshua: “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch”, who will build the temple of the LORD, bear royal honour and be a priest on his throne (vv. 12–13). The crown is laid up in the temple as a reminder, and people far off will come and help to build (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: God crowns a priest as a sign of the coming one who will be king and priest together, and who builds his temple with people from far away.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Take from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, who have arrived from Babylon, and go the same day to the house of Josiah, the son of Zephaniah. Take from them silver and gold, and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua, the son of Jehozadak, the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At God’s command Zechariah makes a crown from gifts sent by exiles in Babylon and sets it, startlingly, on the head of the high priest.

Make a crown. The visions end and an action begins. Three men have arrived from Babylon, presumably carrying gifts from Jews still there, and Zechariah is to act “the same day”. What follows is shocking: the crown goes on the head of Joshua, “the high priest”.

Two offices kept apart. In Israel those two offices were kept strictly apart. Kings came from Judah and David; priests came from Levi and Aaron. When King Uzziah tried to burn incense in the temple he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Here, by God’s own instruction, a crown goes on a priest’s head.

Not Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel, David’s descendant and the obvious candidate, is not crowned. This is a deliberate sign, explained in the next verses.

Gifts from far away. The crown came from the gifts of exiles who had not come home. Believers far away, who would never see this temple, paid for the sign that pointed to Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says “crowns”, plural. It is probably one crown of several bands, as the ESV notes.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to him, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: for he shall branch out from his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD. It is he who shall build the temple of the LORD and shall bear royal honor, and shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowned priest is a sign of the coming Branch, who will build God’s true temple and rule as king and priest at once: Jesus.

Behold, the man whose name is the Branch. “The Branch” again (3:8), the promised king from David’s cut-down family tree (Jeremiah 23:5). Joshua is wearing the crown; the Branch is the one it points to. “He shall build the temple of the LORD”: not this modest building, which Zerubbabel’s hands would finish (4:9), but a greater one.

A priest on his throne. One man will “bear royal honor” and “sit and rule on his throne”, and at the same time be “a priest on his throne”. The two offices that Israel had kept apart for centuries are joined in one person.

One person to rule and reconcile. One of the clearest pictures of Christ in the prophets. We need a king to rule us and a priest to reconcile us, and it would be a poor arrangement if they were two different people who had to agree. In Jesus “the counsel of peace”, the harmony between the two offices, is settled in one person: the one who brings us to God is the one who governs us.

A hint in the Psalms. The Psalms had hinted at this: a king in David’s line addressed as “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), the ancient king of Salem who was also priest of God Most High. Hebrews applies it all to Jesus, who “holds his priesthood permanently” and is “able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him” (Hebrews 7:24–25).

A priest without a throne. Much modern spirituality wants a priest without a throne: a God who comforts, forgives and accepts, but has no right to tell us how to live. Much modern politics, and some religion, wants a throne without a priest: rules, power and moral demands, with no mercy for those who fail them. The first gives us a therapist; the second gives us a tyrant. Neither can save. A priest who cannot rule can only sympathise with what is wrecking you, and a king who cannot reconcile can only condemn you for it. Zechariah’s crown on a priest’s head says that God will not let the two be separated. The one who has every right to command your life is the one who laid down his life to bring you to God, so his authority is never cold and his kindness is never soft. That is why bowing to Jesus feels, to those who do it, less like losing their freedom than like coming to rest.

Where Christians differ. Many modern scholars think the Branch first meant Zerubbabel, who was building the temple (4:9), and that the priest is Joshua beside his throne, with peace between the two men. (The ESV notes the line may read “by his throne”, and the Greek Old Testament has the priest at his right hand.)

This commentary’s view. The Branch here is still to come (3:8), the crown is put on the priest, and no governor built the temple this oracle describes. The New Testament points to the one who is both.
verseByVerse.note: The Branch will be both priest and king, two offices united in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crown shall be in the temple of the LORD as a reminder to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen the son of Zephaniah. "And those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD. And you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall come to pass, if you will diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crown is laid up in the temple as a reminder of a promise not yet kept, and people from far away will come to help build God’s temple, as Gentiles now do in Christ.

The crown shall be in the temple of the LORD. The crown does not stay on Joshua’s head. It is placed in the temple “as a reminder”, hanging there as a promise waiting to be kept.

Names remembered. The men who gave the silver and gold and made the long journey are named twice, a kindness: God put their names in his book.

Those who are far off shall come. The men from Babylon are a sample of something larger: “those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD.” Paul uses that very language of Gentile Christians: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ”, and “you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:13, 22). Every Gentile believer is one of the far-off people helping to build the temple Zechariah saw.

If you will diligently obey. The chapter closes with a condition, in the language of Deuteronomy 28:1. The promise does not wait to be earned; it is made to people God already calls his own, and the condition is how they will come to enjoy it. Their fathers did not obey (1:4), and neither do we as we should. That is why the crown points beyond Joshua to the Branch, the priest-king who obeyed perfectly for his people and now builds them together by his Spirit.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “Helem” is another spelling of Heldai (v. 10). “Hen” means “favour” and is probably another name for Josiah the son of Zephaniah (v. 10), perhaps remembering his kindness in receiving the travellers.

6.title: The Crown and the Branch
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 brings the night visions to a close (vv. 1–8) and then turns from vision to a sign acted out in Jerusalem (vv. 9–15). Sin has just been carried off to Shinar (chapter 5); now the God who has cleansed his people sends out his chariots and crowns his priest.

The message. The Lord of all the earth governs world history, and the King he is bringing will also be a Priest. Every power at work among the nations goes out only at his command, and his purposes press on until his anger against the oppressor is satisfied. At the centre of his plan stands “the man whose name is the Branch”, who will build God’s true temple and rule on his throne as priest and king at once, with builders gathered from far away.

Why it was said. Judah had no king, only a governor of David’s line who answered to Persia, and a high priest serving at a half-built temple (see the introduction). The people needed to know that the empire’s horses did not have the last word, and that God’s promises to David’s house had not shrunk to the size of Zerubbabel and Joshua.

How the chapter makes its case. Four chariots come out from between two bronze mountains (vv. 1–3); they go out to the four winds only after standing before the Lord of all the earth, and those that go north set God’s Spirit at rest there (vv. 4–8). Then Zechariah takes silver and gold brought by exiles from Babylon, makes a crown and sets it on the head of Joshua the high priest (vv. 9–11), with a word about the Branch who will build the temple and be priest and king in one (vv. 12–13). The crown is kept in the temple as a reminder, and people from far off will come to help build, if Judah will obey (vv. 14–15).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise and by pattern. Joshua, a priest wearing a crown, is a living sign of the Branch (3:8), the son of David who is also “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews shows Jesus as exactly that: “we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven” (Hebrews 8:1). He builds the true temple, his people, “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22), with stones brought from far off. And the chariots answer to him: he “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).

For us. The one who has every right to rule our lives is the priest who gave his life to bring us to God, so we can bow to him without fear and come to him without shame. Gentile believers are the far-off people of verse 15, and no gift given and no stone laid in his building is forgotten.
6.theology:
The powers at work in world history move only after reporting before the Lord of all the earth; his agents are eager, and his apparent delay is not inactivity. His purposes press on until wrong is dealt with, and then there is rest (vv. 5-8).

A crown on a priest's head breaks Israel's settled order as a sign of something new (v. 11; 2 Chr 26:16-21): the Branch will be king and priest in one person (v. 13; Ps 110:4; Heb 7:24-25). God records the names of those whose gifts support his work (v. 14), and people from far away help to build his true temple, the Gentiles brought near in Christ (v. 15; Eph 2:13, 22).
6.examples: Chariots issue from between two mountains of bronze, their horses straining at the bit until God says go. Then a crown of silver and gold, made from an offering carried out of Babylon, is set on a priest while the king's heir stands by, and hung in the temple as a reminder of a promise that far-off people would come to help build.

keyVerse.quote: It is he who shall build the temple of the LORD and shall bear royal honor, and shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
keyVerse.note: This verse joins what Israel had always kept apart: the throne of David and the priesthood. The Branch will rule as king and reconcile as priest, and build God’s true temple. Jesus is that one person, seated at God’s right hand as our King and interceding for us as our Priest, so the one who commands our lives is the one who gave his life for us.

6.reflection:
The chariots go out only “after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth” (v. 5), and they are “impatient to go” (v. 7). How does it help to know that the powers at work in the world report to God? Where are you tempted to mistake his timing for inactivity?

A crown on a priest’s head broke all Israel’s rules (vv. 11–13). Why do we need Jesus to be both our King and our Priest? Which do you find easier to welcome, his authority or his mercy, and what happens when one is held without the other?

Exiles who would never see the temple gave the silver and gold for the crown, and their names were remembered (vv. 10, 14). What does that say about gifts and work for God that no one else notices?

“Those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD” (v. 15). How does Ephesians 2:13–22 show this coming true? Who are the far-off people your church could welcome into the building?

7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev.<sup>2</sup>Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to entreat the favor of the LORD,<sup>3</sup>saying to the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD of hosts came to me:<sup>5</sup>"Say to all the people of the land and the priests, 'When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?<sup>6</sup>And when you eat and when you drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?<sup>7</sup>Were not these the words that the LORD proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, with her cities around her, and the South and the lowland were inhabited?'"<sup>8</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another,<sup>10</sup>do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart."<sup>11</sup>But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears that they might not hear.<sup>12</sup>They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law and the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of hosts.<sup>13</sup>"As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear," says the LORD of hosts,<sup>14</sup>"and I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known. Thus the land they left was desolate, so that no one went to and fro, and the pleasant land was made desolate."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God asks of every religious habit the one question that matters: who is it for? Almost two years after the visions, men come from Bethel to ask the priests and prophets whether they should go on weeping and fasting in the fifth month, as they have done “for so many years” (vv. 1–3). God does not answer yes or no. He asks the people and the priests whether their fasts, in the fifth month and the seventh, were ever really for him, and whether their eating and drinking were not simply for themselves (vv. 4–6). None of this is new: the former prophets said it while Jerusalem was still prosperous and the land full of people (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God asks of every religious habit the one question that matters: who is it for?

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev. Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to entreat the favor of the LORD, saying to the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Almost two years after the visions, a delegation from Bethel asks whether they should still keep the fast that mourned the temple’s destruction, now that it is being rebuilt.

In the fourth year of King Darius. November or December 518 BC. The temple is rising, and despair has given way to something like normality.

Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month? During the exile the people had kept several fasts mourning the disasters. The fast of “the fifth month” marked the burning of the temple by the Babylonians (2 Kings 25:8–9). Now the temple is nearly rebuilt. Should the mourning continue?

A tradition God never commanded. The question, of the kind any church committee might ask, concerns a fast God never commanded: their own tradition, seventy years old and deeply felt. Where the question came from is worth noticing. Bethel had once housed Jeroboam’s golden calf, the rival shrine that drew the northern tribes away from Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:28–29); now men from Bethel bring their question to “the house of the LORD of hosts”.

Uncertain wording. Verse 2 can also be read “Bethel-sharezer had sent Regem-melech and his men”, making Bethel-sharezer a man’s name rather than the town; either way a delegation comes to Jerusalem with a question. “To entreat the favor of the LORD” is literally “to soften the face of the LORD”, a common idiom for seeking his goodwill.
verseByVerse.note: Bethel, where the delegation came from, lay about twelve miles north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD of hosts came to me: "Say to all the people of the land and the priests, 'When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted? And when you eat and when you drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves? Were not these the words that the LORD proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, with her cities around her, and the South and the lowland were inhabited?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not answer yes or no; he asks whether their fasting, and their feasting, were ever really for him.

In the fifth month and in the seventh. God widens the question to a second fast. The fast of the seventh month probably mourned the murder of Gedaliah, the governor left in charge after Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:25).

Was it for me that you fasted? Seventy years of genuine grief, and God asks whom it was really for. They had mourned a burnt building and their own suffering; had they mourned their sin, or had it been a national ritual of self-pity? And their feasts were the same: “do you not eat for yourselves?”

By the former prophets. God points them back to the prophets who said this while Jerusalem was still “inhabited and prosperous” (compare Isaiah 58:3–7). The tragedy is that they are asking about fast days rather than about the justice and mercy the prophets actually demanded (vv. 9–10).

Jesus and fasting. Jesus pressed the same question. He warned against fasting to be seen (Matthew 6:16–18), and when asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark 2:19). With Christ present, the old mourning gives way to joy, which is where Zechariah’s answer is heading (8:19).

Who is it for? That question can be asked of any religious habit: the quiet time, the church attendance, the giving, the abstaining. If our fasting and our feasting are both for ourselves, God has not really come into it. Paul puts the positive version: “whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

What it does not mean. Not that fasting or religious custom is wrong. Jesus assumed his disciples would fast (“when you fast”, Matthew 6:16), and the early church fasted and prayed (Acts 13:2–3). The question is not whether, but for whom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Words They Would Not Hear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God wanted mercy and justice, not mourning ceremonies, and a people who refuse to listen will in the end call and not be heard. The word God sent by the former prophets was plain: render true judgments, show kindness and mercy, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner or the poor, and do not plot evil against one another even in the heart (vv. 8–10). But the fathers refused, turned a stubborn shoulder, stopped their ears and made their hearts diamond-hard against words sent by God’s Spirit (vv. 11–12). So, as he called and they would not hear, they called and he would not hear; he scattered them among the nations and the pleasant land was left desolate (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: God wanted mercy and justice, not mourning ceremonies, and refusing to listen finally silences the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God always wanted was not ceremonies but honest judgments, practical kindness, protection for the defenceless and hearts that plot no harm.

Render true judgments. Startlingly concrete: honest decisions in court and in daily dealings, and “kindness and mercy to one another”, the practical goodness that makes a community liveable. Then four groups: the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner and the poor, people with no husband, no father, no citizenship and no money, the four classic ways of being defenceless in that world.

Let none of you devise evil. And finally the inward command: “let none of you devise evil against another in your heart”. God’s law reaches even what we imagine and plan, because that is where injustice is designed.

The same summary elsewhere. Micah had summed it up: “to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). James says pure religion is “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). The test of real religion has never changed, and it is never merely what we abstain from.

Not the price of his favour. These commands were spoken to people God had brought back from exile and called his own; they are the shape of life with him, not the price of his favour. None of us has kept them as we should, and Christ, who never once despised the poor or devised evil in his heart, kept them perfectly in our place. Forgiven for his sake, we are given his Spirit, who makes us merciful as he is.

What this looks like. Decide truly. On the interview panel, the school report, the dispute between two friends, judge the case on its merits, not on who is asking. Be kind in small, costly ways. The meal for the new mother, the lift for the neighbour who no longer drives, patience with the slow colleague. Know your widow, orphan, stranger and poor. Most churches have all four within reach: the widow who eats alone on Sundays, the child from a broken home, the overseas student, the family behind on the rent. Learn one name and do one thing for them this month. Watch what you rehearse. When your mind starts planning how to get even or get ahead at someone’s expense, stop and pray for that person instead. We can live like this because God did it first: when we were the defenceless ones, Christ came for us. So Paul says, “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

verseByVerse.quote: But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears that they might not hear. They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law and the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of hosts. "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear," says the LORD of hosts, "and I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known. Thus the land they left was desolate, so that no one went to and fro, and the pleasant land was made desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fathers refused God’s word until their hearts were as hard as diamond, so when they cried out he did not answer, and the land was left desolate.

They refused to pay attention. Three pictures of refusal, each worse than the last. They “refused to pay attention”. They “turned a stubborn shoulder”, like an ox wrenching its shoulder out from under the yoke. And they “stopped their ears”.

They made their hearts diamond-hard. Deepest of all, and they did it themselves. Hardness of heart is manufactured, decision by decision, until nothing gets in. And they were refusing not good advice but words “the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets”. Stephen would say the same of a later generation: “you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

As I called, and they would not hear. Verse 13 has a terrible symmetry. The generation that would not listen eventually needed God to listen, and found silence. This is not God sulking but the settled consequence of a life lived deaf to him, which is why every call of God is urgent while it can still be heard: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–8).

The cure for a hard heart. There is only one cure for a diamond-hard heart, and it is not effort. God promises it: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). What we cannot soften, he can replace. And the silence the fathers met was met once more at the cross, when the Son cried “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46); he bore that silence so that no one who calls on him now will be turned away. Anyone afraid that his heart has grown too hard may take comfort from the fear itself: a diamond-hard heart does not worry about hearing God.

The answer to the delegation. You are asking whether to keep mourning the ruin; ask instead why it happened, and make sure this generation is not like the last. Then read chapter 8, where God turns all four fasts into feasts.

Uncertain wording. “Stopped their ears” is literally “made their ears too heavy to hear”, as the ESV notes. The word rendered “diamond” is also translated “emery” (Ezekiel 3:9); it is the hardest stone the writer knew. In verse 13 the ESV notes that the Hebrew has “he” where the ESV has “I”; the speaker is God either way.

7.title: Was It for Me That You Fasted?
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 7 and 8 come almost two years after the night visions, late in 518 BC, while the temple is rising (v. 1; see the introduction). A question about fasting from the town of Bethel opens a new section, and God’s answer runs through both chapters; chapter 7 is its hard half.

The message. God cares less about our religious calendar than about whom our religion is for and how we treat one another. He asks of a fast kept for seventy years, “was it for me?”, and points back to what he always wanted: honest judgments, kindness and mercy, and no oppression of the defenceless. Their fathers refused to listen until their hearts were as hard as diamond, and the ruin the fast mourned was the result.

Why it was said. With the temple nearly rebuilt, the people of Bethel asked whether they might stop mourning its destruction. The question showed how easily the returned community could keep up religious habits while missing the lesson of the exile.

How the chapter makes its case. The delegation asks about the fast of the fifth month (vv. 1–3). God answers with questions: was your fasting for me, and is not your eating for yourselves? The former prophets said all this before (vv. 4–7). Then he repeats their message: true judgments, kindness and mercy, care for the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner and the poor, and no evil plotted in the heart (vv. 8–10). The fathers refused, stopped their ears and hardened their hearts, so when they called God did not hear, and the pleasant land was left desolate (vv. 11–14). The happy answer, fasts turned into feasts, waits in chapter 8.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. Israel’s religion was hollow and her heart was hard, and no fast could cure either. Jesus fasted for his Father, not for show (Matthew 4:2; 6:16–18), kept the law of mercy perfectly, and became himself the defenceless one oppressed (Isaiah 53:7). On the cross he took the silence of an unanswered cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that those who call on him will be heard; and he gives the new heart God promised (Ezekiel 36:26).

For us. Ask of every religious habit whom it is really for, and measure your faith less by what you give up than by mercy shown to people who cannot repay. And do not delay when God speaks: hardness grows one refusal at a time, but whoever fears that his heart is too hard has not yet stopped hearing.
7.theology:
God asks of every religious habit who it is actually for, because costly religion can be entirely self-centred (vv. 5-6; 1 Cor 10:31). What he has always wanted is true judgment, kindness and mercy, and protection for the defenceless, with commands that reach the imagination where injustice is designed (vv. 9-10; Mic 6:8; Jas 1:27).

Hardness of heart is manufactured by repeated refusals and ends in the silence of unanswered prayer; only God can replace such a heart (vv. 11-13; Ezek 36:26).
7.examples: A delegation asks whether a seventy-year-old tradition can now stop, and is answered with a better question: were the fasting and the feasting both for themselves, with God in neither? Four kinds of defenceless people are named in one sentence. Then comes an ox wrenching its shoulder out from under the yoke, hearts made as hard as diamond one refusal at a time, and a generation that would not hear and then was not heard.

keyVerse.quote: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?
keyVerse.note: God answers a question about the religious calendar with a question about the heart. Seventy years of sincere mourning are weighed by one test: was it for him? The question searches every habit of devotion, and drives us to Christ, the one whose every act of worship was wholly for his Father, and in whom our poor offerings are accepted.

7.reflection:
God answers the question about fasting with “was it for me that you fasted?” (v. 5). Think of one religious habit in your life or your church. Who is it really for, and how could you tell?

Verses 9–10 name four kinds of defenceless people. Who are the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner and the poor in your neighbourhood or church today, and what is one concrete thing your group could do for one of them?

“Let none of you devise evil against another in your heart” (v. 10). Why does God’s law reach into our imagination and planning? What do you tend to rehearse in your mind, and how could you turn it into prayer?

The fathers “made their hearts diamond-hard” one refusal at a time (vv. 11–12). How does a heart harden in practice? What hope do Ezekiel 36:26 and the cross give to someone who fears his heart has grown hard?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — I Have Returned to Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s fierce love brings him back to live among his people, and his restoration is measured by the safety of the very old and the very young. He is jealous for Zion with great jealousy (vv. 1–2); he has returned and will dwell in Jerusalem, which will be called the faithful city and the holy mountain (v. 3). The promise is beautifully ordinary: old men and women sitting in the streets with sticks in their hands, and the streets full of boys and girls playing (vv. 4–5). If that seems impossible to the remnant, need it seem impossible to God? (v. 6). He will bring his people home from east and west, “and they shall be my people, and I will be their God” (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promise of restoration is measured in old people sitting safely and children playing in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD of hosts came, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. Thus says the LORD: I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the faithful city, and the mountain of the LORD of hosts, the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s fierce love for Zion brings him back to live among his people, and the city once notorious for unfaithfulness will be called the faithful city.

I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy. Chapter 8 answers chapter 7’s desolation with ten messages, each beginning “Thus says the LORD”, and the first is about God’s own heart. He is “jealous for Zion”, with the fierce protectiveness of a husband who will not share his wife or let her be harmed; the “great wrath” is turned on those who would harm her. This is not petty envy but covenant love that will not let go (Exodus 34:14).

Jerusalem shall be called the faithful city. “I have returned to Zion”: the promise of 1:16 restated. And the city will get a new name, “the faithful city”. Isaiah had cried, “How the faithful city has become a whore” (Isaiah 1:21). God intends to give the title back, and the city will be “the holy mountain” because he lives there.

God with us. “I … will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem” was fulfilled beyond anything the remnant imagined when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and it will be complete when “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with staff in hand because of great age. And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in its streets. Thus says the LORD of hosts: If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight, declares the LORD of hosts? Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, I will save my people from the east country and from the west country, and I will bring them to dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in faithfulness and in righteousness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s picture of restored peace is ordinary and beautiful: old people sitting safely and children playing in the streets; and what seems impossible to his people is not impossible to him.

Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets. Not victory parades or gold, but old men and women sitting out with their walking sticks, and “boys and girls playing”. The very old and the very young are the first to suffer when a society is violent, so a city where they sit and play safely in public is a city at peace. That is what God promises, and what he counts as a great blessing.

What makes a city good? Ask how a modern city is doing and you will usually hear about growth, investment and new buildings. Zechariah measures it by its oldest and youngest. The urban writer Jane Jacobs, in The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961), argued along similar lines: a street is healthy when ordinary people of every age use it and keep an eye on it, so that children can play on the pavement under many watchful eyes. A culture can be rich and still be the kind of place where the old are hidden away and children are few or kept indoors, because both are slow, costly and unproductive. God’s picture of flourishing is gloriously inefficient: it has room for those who can no longer work and those who cannot yet. That is because his own kingdom works that way. Jesus took children in his arms when his disciples tried to send them off (Mark 10:13–16), and the aged Simeon and Anna were among the first to welcome him in the temple (Luke 2:25–38). In his city nobody is valued for their output.

If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant. To the little community it all seemed impossible. God’s reply is gentle: it may look “marvelous”, that is, beyond possibility, to you; must it therefore be so to me? The same question was asked of Abraham and Sarah, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14), and the angel said to Mary, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).

They shall be my people. God will gather them from east and west, and the covenant words return: “they shall be my people, and I will be their God”. That sentence runs through the Bible, from Sinai to the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33) and on to the last page, where God dwells with his people for ever (Revelation 21:3).

In faithfulness and in righteousness. The two words at the end matter. This is not sentimental restoration that overlooks sin; God restores justly, and for us that means through the cross, where sin was dealt with.

Where Christians differ. How is this return fulfilled? Its first fulfilment was the return from Babylon, still under way as Zechariah spoke. Dispensational Christians expect a further gathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it beginning in the modern state of Israel. Yet the promise here is larger than territory: God dwelling among his people, a covenant kept “in faithfulness and in righteousness”.

This commentary’s view. The New Testament sees that gathering in Christ, who brings his scattered sheep from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), and Paul, as many read him, foresees a great turning of Jewish people to their Messiah (Romans 11:26). It will be complete in the new creation. This commentary reads the promise as fulfilled in Christ because the New Testament itself applies Israel’s hopes to his one people, while honouring brothers and sisters who expect more in the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Let Your Hands Be Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promises are meant to strengthen his people for the work, and his blessing comes with a plain ethic. “Let your hands be strong,” he tells the builders (v. 9). Before, there was no wage and no safety, and he himself set neighbour against neighbour (v. 10); but now there will be a sowing of peace, a fruitful land and dew from heaven (vv. 11–12), and a people that had been a byword of cursing will be a blessing (v. 13). As surely as God purposed disaster and did not relent, he has now purposed good (vv. 14–15). So speak the truth, give judgments that are true and make for peace, plot no evil and love no false oath, for God hates all these (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promised blessing comes with a plain ethic: truthful speech, honest courts and no scheming.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Let your hands be strong, you who in these days have been hearing these words from the mouth of the prophets who were present on the day that the foundation of the house of the LORD of hosts was laid, that the temple might be built. For before those days there was no wage for man or any wage for beast, neither was there any safety from the foe for him who went out or came in, for I set every man against his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the tired builders to be strong, reminding them of the hardship and division that came while his house lay neglected.

Let your hands be strong. This is the encouragement of a foreman to tired builders, who have been hearing these promises from “the prophets”, Haggai and Zechariah, since the work restarted (Ezra 5:1–2). God’s promises are given while the work is in progress, to strengthen people for it.

I set every man against his neighbor. Verse 10 sums up Haggai’s diagnosis (Haggai 1:6–11) in a sentence: no wages, no security, no neighbourliness. And God says he himself caused it. When a community turns from God, the fractures between people are part of the judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, declares the LORD of hosts. For there shall be a sowing of peace. The vine shall give its fruit, and the ground shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew. And I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things. And as you have been a byword of cursing among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so will I save you, and you shall be a blessing. Fear not, but let your hands be strong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now God turns everything around: a sowing of peace, a fruitful land, and a people once a byword for curse made a blessing.

There shall be a sowing of peace. “But now”: the turn comes. The seed goes in and what comes up is peace. Vine, ground and heavens all give again (compare Haggai 2:19).

You shall be a blessing. They had been a “byword of cursing”, the nation others pointed at as an example of ruin. Now, “you shall be a blessing”, which was God’s word to Abraham at the very beginning (Genesis 12:2). It comes true in Christ, “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14).

Fear not, but let your hands be strong. The call to work comes after the promise, not before it: God’s “I will save you” is the ground, and their work is the response. His promises are not an invitation to sit still.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent, says the LORD of hosts, so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not. These are the things that you shall do: Speak the truth to one another; render in your gates judgments that are true and make for peace; do not devise evil in your hearts against one another, and love no false oath, for all these things I hate, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who kept his word in judgment will keep it in blessing, and his people are to answer with truthful speech, honest courts and hearts free of scheming.

I did not relent. God argues from his own track record, and it is a surprising argument. You know I do what I say, because I did the terrible thing I promised and “did not relent”. The exile proved that God’s word holds. So when he promises “good”, expect the same reliability. A believer can use this: the sharpest evidence that God keeps his word may be some discipline we have been through. The God who was that serious about his warnings is that serious about his promises.

Speak the truth to one another. The response God asks is startlingly down to earth. Paul quotes this line to the church at Ephesus as basic Christian behaviour: “let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25). And “render in your gates” (the city gate was the town’s courtroom) “judgments that are true and make for peace”, because justice is meant to heal a community, not merely to settle scores.

For all these things I hate. Then the heart: “do not devise evil in your hearts”, and no false oaths, “for all these things I hate”: lies, crooked judgments, private scheming and perjury, the sins of ordinary dealings.

Where we have failed. Every one of us has failed here, in word and in heart. The way back is the one this chapter opens: God has purposed good for his people, and in Christ, who spoke only truth, that good is ours, with forgiveness for every lie confessed. The Spirit he gives makes truthful speech possible, which is why Paul grounds the same command in our new life in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns his people’s mourning into feasting, and makes them the people others follow to find him. The Bethel question is answered at last: the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months will become seasons of joy and gladness, so love truth and peace (vv. 18–19). Then the horizon widens to the whole world. People from many cities will urge one another to go and seek the LORD, each saying, “I myself am going” (vv. 20–22). And ten men from the nations will take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God turns his people's mourning into feasting, and makes them the people others follow to find him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD of hosts came to me, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth and the fast of the seventh and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the Bethel question at last: all four fasts of mourning will become joyful feasts, so his people should love truth and peace.

The fast of the fourth month. The delegation asked about one fast; God answers about all four. The fourth month marked the breach of Jerusalem’s wall, the fifth the burning of the temple, the seventh the murder of Gedaliah, and the tenth the start of the siege (2 Kings 25:1–25). And he does not say “stop”. He says they will become “seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts”.

Seasons of joy and gladness. That is how God deals with his people’s grief. He does not tell them to forget it or to keep observing it for ever; he turns it into gladness. The days that marked the worst events in their history become festivals.

Good Friday. Christians know the greatest instance of this. The day of the most terrible event in history, the killing of God’s Son, is the day Christians call Good Friday. Jesus promised his grieving disciples, “your sorrow will turn into joy” (John 16:20).

Therefore love truth and peace. The gladness comes first, and the response is not “keep the right feasts” but love the things God loves.

Dreaded anniversaries. The God who can do that with a calendar can do it with a life. Anniversaries that have been dreaded for years are not beyond his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Peoples shall yet come, even the inhabitants of many cities. The inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, 'Let us go at once to entreat the favor of the LORD and to seek the LORD of hosts; I myself am going.' Many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the favor of the LORD. Thus says the LORD of hosts: In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations will come to seek the LORD, urging one another on and holding on to his people, because they have heard that God is with them.

I myself am going. People in one city call on their neighbours in the next: “Let us go at once”, and then the personal commitment, “I myself am going”. Nobody is coerced. This is the spread of genuine spiritual hunger, and it begins with individuals who will not wait.

We have heard that God is with you. The middle section of the book (chapters 7–8) ends with this picture. Ten men, a way of saying many, grab hold of a Jewish man’s robe and beg to be taken along, because “we have heard that God is with you”. The word for “robe” means the corner of the garment, where Israelites wore the tassels that reminded them of God’s commands (Numbers 15:38–39); to take hold of it was probably to attach oneself to that man and to his God.

Salvation from the Jews. It happened. Salvation came to the world through the Jewish people, as Jesus told the Samaritan woman: “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). Gentiles who were “strangers to the covenants of promise” have been “brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:12–13), and today most Christians on earth are among those who took hold of the robe. In the Gospels the sick begged to “touch even the fringe of his garment” (Matthew 14:36): in the end the Jew whose robe the nations grasp is Jesus himself, Immanuel, the one in whom God is with us.

What still draws people. The reason still stands. What draws people is not our arguments or our buildings but the report that God is with us. That was the promise of 2:10 and 8:3, and it remains the church’s only real attraction.

8.title: Old Men and Children in the Streets
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 completes God’s answer to the men from Bethel (7:1–3). Chapter 7 ended with a desolate land and a people who would not hear; now ten short messages, each opening “Thus says the LORD”, pour out promises, and the question about fasting is answered at last (vv. 18–19).

The message. God is so committed to his people that he will come and live among them, make their broken city safe for the very old and the very young, turn their curse into blessing and their days of mourning into feasts, and draw the nations to himself through them. What seems impossible to a weak remnant is not impossible to him, and the God who kept his word in judgment will keep it in mercy. His people are to answer with strong hands, truthful speech and honest courts.

Why it was said. The returned community was small, poor and still haunted by its losses: the empty streets, the failed harvests, the danger on the roads (v. 10) and the yearly fasts for its disasters (see the introduction). They needed to hear what God intended for them, and to be strengthened to keep building.

How the chapter makes its case. God is jealous for Zion and has returned to dwell in her (vv. 1–3); old people and children will fill her streets, which is not too marvellous for him (vv. 4–6); he will gather his people and be their God (vv. 7–8). So let your hands be strong: the years of no wage and no safety give way to a sowing of peace, and a byword of cursing becomes a blessing (vv. 9–13). As he purposed disaster and did not relent, he now purposes good, so speak the truth and judge truly (vv. 14–17). The four fasts become feasts (vv. 18–19), and the nations come seeking the LORD, ten men holding the robe of one Jew because God is with him (vv. 20–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise. The God who says “I … will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem” came to live among us in his Son: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and he will dwell with his people for ever (Revelation 21:3). Through one Jewish man the nations have come to God, for “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22), and Gentiles once far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). The covenant promise “they shall be my people, and I will be their God” is kept “in faithfulness and in righteousness” at the cross, and the fasts of mourning become feasts because the Bridegroom has come (Mark 2:19).

For us. God’s promises are given to strengthen tired hands for the work in front of them. A church shows that God is with her not by her size but by truthfulness, justice and joy, and those are what make outsiders want to come along. And the God who turned a nation’s darkest anniversaries into festivals can do the same with ours.
8.theology:
God is jealous for his people, and his measure of a restored society is the safety of the very old and the very young (vv. 2-5). What seems impossible to his people is not impossible to him (v. 6; Luke 1:37), and he keeps his covenant, "my people ... their God", in faithfulness and righteousness (v. 8; Jer 31:33; Rev 21:3). The reliability he showed in his warnings is the measure of the reliability of his promises (vv. 14-15).

His blessing calls for truthful speech, honest courts and hearts that scheme no evil (vv. 16-17). He turns the anniversaries of his people's worst griefs into feasts (v. 19), and the nations come to him through the people he is with, as Gentiles are brought near in Christ (vv. 20-23; John 4:22; Eph 2:12-13).
8.examples: Old people with walking sticks sit out in the street again, and the streets are too safe to keep the children indoors: a promise that looks impossible to everyone except God. A sowing yields a crop of peace, and four fast days become four festivals. One neighbour says to another, "I myself am going", and strangers hold the hem of a coat and ask to come along.

keyVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, ‘Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’
keyVerse.note: The chapter, and the whole answer to Bethel, ends with the nations streaming to God through the people he lives among. It came true when the nations came to God through Jesus, the Jew in whom God is with us, and it still describes what makes a church attractive: not size or skill, but the report that God is with her.

8.reflection:
God measures a restored city by old people sitting safely and children playing in the streets (vv. 4–5). What would it look like for your church or neighbourhood to make room for those who can no longer work and those who cannot yet?

“If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant … should it also be marvelous in my sight?” (v. 6). What do you find hard to believe God could do, in your life or your church? How do Genesis 18:14 and Luke 1:37 speak to that?

God’s blessing comes with plain commands: speak the truth, judge fairly, plot no evil, love no false oath (vv. 16–17). Why do these ordinary matters show so clearly whether God is with a people? Which is hardest for you?

The fasts that marked Israel’s worst days become feasts (v. 19), and the nations come because “we have heard that God is with you” (v. 23). Is there a dreaded day or memory you can bring to God in hope? What would make outsiders say this about your church?
