verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Oracle Against the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the King arrives, the LORD clears his road and guards his house. His word of judgment moves down the map: Hadrach, Damascus and Hamath in the north, then Tyre and Sidon, “though they are very wise”, whose rampart and heaped silver cannot save them (vv. 1–4). The Philistine cities watch and tremble, and their pride is cut off (vv. 5–6). Then comes the surprise: God ends Philistia’s idol feasts, and it too “shall be a remnant for our God”, like “a clan in Judah” (v. 7). Finally God camps at his house as its guard, so that no oppressor will march over his people again, “for now I see with my own eyes” (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God judges the proud nations and then takes some of them into his own family, while guarding his people himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle of the word of the LORD is against the land of Hadrach and Damascus is its resting place. For the LORD has an eye on mankind and on all the tribes of Israel, and on Hamath also, which borders on it, Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise. Tyre has built herself a rampart and heaped up silver like dust, and fine gold like the mud of the streets. But behold, the Lord will strip her of her possessions and strike down her power on the sea, and she shall be devoured by fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD’s judgment falls on the rich, clever cities north of Israel, and Tyre, trusting in her walls and wealth, will be stripped and burned.

The oracle of the word of the LORD. An oracle (literally “a burden”) is a weighty message, and this one opens the book’s closing oracles (see the introduction). It tours the map from the north: Hadrach, Damascus and Hamath in Syria, on the edge of the land once promised to Israel (Numbers 34:8). The word lands on Damascus and stays.

The LORD has an eye on mankind. God watches all peoples, not only Israel; nations that never gave him a thought are under his eye.

Tyre has built herself a rampart. Tyre, with Sidon, was the great trading port, famously clever and rich: “silver like dust, and fine gold like the mud of the streets”. Her island fortress had outlasted siege after siege, but she “shall be devoured by fire”. Alexander the Great took the city in 332 BC by building a causeway to the island, and his march followed this oracle’s route, from Syria down the coast to Gaza; many readers see a first fulfilment there.

No defence against God. Cleverness and money are no defence against God, and he is not judging at random: he is clearing the road for his King (v. 9).

Uncertain wording. Hadrach appears nowhere else in the Bible, but Assyrian records name a region called Hatarikka near Hamath, very likely the place. And “the LORD has an eye on mankind” can also be read, as the ESV notes, “For the eye of mankind, especially of all the tribes of Israel, is toward the LORD”. Either God watches all peoples, or all peoples will look to him.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 9–14 look further ahead, to the coming King and the final day.

verseByVerse.quote: Ashkelon shall see it, and be afraid; Gaza too, and shall writhe in anguish; Ekron also, because its hopes are confounded. The king shall perish from Gaza; Ashkelon shall be uninhabited; a mixed people shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of Philistia. I will take away its blood from its mouth, and its abominations from between its teeth; it too shall be a remnant for our God; it shall be like a clan in Judah, and Ekron shall be like the Jebusites. Then I will encamp at my house as a guard, so that none shall march to and fro; no oppressor shall again march over them, for now I see with my own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistine cities will be humbled and their idolatry ended, and then, astonishingly, Philistia will be adopted into God’s people while God himself guards his house.

Ashkelon shall see it, and be afraid. The Philistine cities watch Tyre, the strength they leaned on, fall and panic. Gaza loses its king, Ashkelon its people, and God cuts off “the pride of Philistia”.

I will take away its blood from its mouth. God snatches its pagan feasts, meat with the blood and unclean food, from between its teeth.

It too shall be a remnant for our God. Here is the surprise that changes the oracle. Philistia, the people of Goliath, becomes “like a clan in Judah”, an ordinary family among God’s people, and “Ekron shall be like the Jebusites”, the people of Jerusalem before David took it, who lived on among Israel (2 Samuel 24:18–24).

The gospel in advance. God does not only defeat his enemies; he converts and adopts them. Jesus healed the daughter of a woman from the region of Tyre and Sidon (Mark 7:24–30), and Philip preached the gospel at Azotus, the old Ashdod (Acts 8:40). Every Christian from a pagan background is an instance of this promise.

I will encamp at my house as a guard. God camps beside his house like a sentry, so the small temple they had built is guarded by God himself. “Now I see with my own eyes”: he has been watching all along.

Was this promise broken? Jerusalem was attacked again, and in AD 70 its temple was destroyed. Like much in these oracles, the promise looks beyond the near future to the final safety of God’s people (see the introduction), secured in Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28).

Uncertain wording. The word for “a mixed people” (v. 6) occurs elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 23:2, of a child of a forbidden union; the ESV notes “a foreign people”. Either way, Ashdod’s proud identity is gone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Your King Comes, Humble on a Donkey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zion’s King comes, and he comes to make peace and set prisoners free. The city is told to shout for joy, because her king is coming to her, righteous, bringing salvation, humble and riding a donkey (v. 9). He breaks the weapons of his own people, speaks peace to the nations and rules to the ends of the earth (v. 10). Because of “the blood of my covenant”, God frees his captives from the waterless pit and calls these “prisoners of hope” back to their stronghold with a promise of double (vv. 11–12). Then he takes up Judah and Ephraim as his bow and arrow against the sons of Greece (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The king comes in humility, disarms his own people, rules the world and frees prisoners by the blood of his covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations; his rule shall be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion is to shout for joy because her true King is coming to her, righteous, bringing salvation and riding humbly on a donkey; he will end war, disarming even his own people, and rule the whole earth by speaking peace.

Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! The reason for joy is not a victory or a harvest but a person arriving: “your king is coming to you”, not summoning them to him but coming to them. Judah had had no king since 586 BC, and Zerubbabel was only a Persian governor. God promises that David’s throne will not stay empty.

Righteous and having salvation is he. Four things are said of him. He is righteous: everything he does is right. He arrives bringing rescue, not demanding it. He is humble. And he rides a donkey.

Mounted on a donkey. A conquering king rode a war horse; a donkey was the mount of a man coming in peace. The words also echo Jacob’s blessing of Judah, whose royal ruler binds “his donkey’s colt to the choice vine” (Genesis 49:11): this is Judah’s promised King, coming in lowliness.

The entry into Jerusalem. On the Sunday before he died, Jesus sent for a colt and rode it into Jerusalem while crowds spread their cloaks on the road. Matthew says this took place “to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet” (Matthew 21:4–5), and John adds that the disciples understood only later that “these things had been written about him” (John 12:15–16). And the humility was not a costume: the King on the donkey was crucified that Friday.

I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim. Look whose weapons are destroyed: not the enemy’s, but “the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem”. God’s own people are disarmed, because their King needs no chariots and their safety no longer rests on weapons.

He shall speak peace to the nations. His weapon is his word, and his rule runs “from sea to sea, and from the River” (the Euphrates, as the ESV notes) “to the ends of the earth”. That is happening now wherever the gospel is preached, for Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far off” (Ephesians 2:17). His kingdom is not spread by force; whenever the church has used force, it has been untrue to its King.

Whose side is God on? In his second inaugural address in 1865, Abraham Lincoln observed that both sides in the American Civil War “read the same Bible and pray to the same God, and each invokes His aid against the other.” Zechariah’s King will not be recruited like that: the first weapons he breaks are his own people’s. He comes not to take a side in our quarrels but to end them, by riding in humbly to be put to death by Jew and Gentile together (Acts 4:27). Peace with God is made at his expense, and then peace between enemies becomes possible, because “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

One animal or two? “A donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” is Hebrew parallelism, one animal described twice. Matthew adds that the colt’s mother came too (Matthew 21:2, 7), natural for a colt never ridden; when he says Jesus sat “on them”, the nearest thing named is the cloaks, not two donkeys at once.

How Jewish readers take it. Rashi says the verse can only be explained of the King Messiah, and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) sets the lowly rider on a donkey beside the son of man coming with the clouds (Daniel 7:13). Jewish readers add, fairly, that the King of verse 10 ends war, and the world is not yet at peace. This commentary sees the King already come in Jesus, and his rule of peace spreading through the gospel until he comes again (Acts 1:11).

Uncertain wording. The word behind “having salvation” is literally passive, “saved” or “delivered”: either a king whom God has rescued and vindicated, or (as the ancient Greek translation took it) one who brings salvation. Both are true of Jesus, vindicated in his resurrection and the Saviour of his people.
verseByVerse.note: When Solomon was proclaimed king, he rode to his anointing on David's own mule (1 Kgs 1:33).

verseByVerse.quote: As for you also, because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit. Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope; today I declare that I will restore to you double. For I have bent Judah as my bow; I have made Ephraim its arrow. I will stir up your sons, O Zion, against your sons, O Greece, and wield you like a warrior's sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the covenant sealed in blood, God will free his captive people from the pit, call them home as “prisoners of hope” with a double blessing, and wield them as his weapons.

The waterless pit. A dry cistern used as a dungeon, impossible to climb out of. Joseph was thrown into one, “empty; there was no water in it” (Genesis 37:24), and so was Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:6). It pictures the Jews still scattered in exile, and every hopeless captivity.

The blood of my covenant with you. At Sinai Moses threw blood on the people and said, “Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8). God had bound himself to them in blood, and he keeps his word.

The cup of the covenant. On the night before he died, Jesus took a cup and said, “this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). That is how prisoners leave the pit: not by climbing, but by blood. God brought Jesus himself up from the dead “by the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20), and his people rise with him.

O prisoners of hope. People still in the pit, but with hope, because a promise has been made: the Christian life exactly, lived between promise and completion. And the promise is “double”, as in Isaiah: “Instead of your shame there shall be a double portion” (Isaiah 61:7). God’s restorations are never grudging.

I have bent Judah as my bow. God takes his people as his weapons: Judah the bow, Ephraim (the lost northern tribes, not forgotten) the arrow, Zion the sword. Greece is a remarkable name in the Persian period (see the introduction), and many readers see a first fulfilment in the Maccabean victories of the 160s BC over the Greek kings of Syria who had defiled the temple.

The church’s weapons. Under the new covenant our weapons are not swords, for “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12). But God still does his work in the world through his people, and he is the one wielding them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The LORD Will Save Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD himself fights for his people, then cares for them as their shepherd and delights in them as his treasure. He appears over them like a storm, his arrow flashing like lightning and his trumpet sounding (v. 14). He protects them, and their victory feast overflows like the bowls at the altar (v. 15). Then the warrior becomes a shepherd: “the LORD their God will save them, as the flock of his people”, and they shine on his land “like the jewels of a crown” (v. 16). The chapter ends in wonder at God’s goodness and beauty, with young men and women flourishing on grain and new wine (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God fights for his people and then wears them like jewels in a crown.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD will appear over them, and his arrow will go forth like lightning; the Lord GOD will sound the trumpet and will march forth in the whirlwinds of the south. The LORD of hosts will protect them, and they shall devour, and tread down the sling stones, and they shall drink and roar as if drunk with wine, and be full like a bowl, drenched like the corners of the altar. On that day the LORD their God will save them, as the flock of his people; for like the jewels of a crown they shall shine on his land. For how great is his goodness, and how great his beauty! Grain shall make the young men flourish, and new wine the young women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD will appear as a warrior to save his people, then gather them as his flock and display them as his treasure, and the chapter ends in wonder at his goodness and beauty.

His arrow will go forth like lightning. The scene becomes a storm. God appears over his people, his arrow flashing, blows the trumpet himself and marches out in the whirlwinds of the south, the direction from which he once came at Sinai (Deuteronomy 33:2).

Full like a bowl. The imagery is rough and jubilant: the enemy’s sling stones trodden underfoot, and the victors as loud as men at a feast, “full like a bowl” used for the blood of sacrifices, “drenched like the corners of the altar”.

As the flock of his people. Then the tone changes completely. The people God has just wielded as weapons are “the flock of his people”, saved by their shepherd. That theme fills the next two chapters and finds its answer in Jesus, the good shepherd who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

Like the jewels of a crown. God wears his people as a king wears his crown jewels. A community struggling with a half-built temple is his public treasure, his “treasured possession” (Malachi 3:17).

How great is his goodness, and how great his beauty! After all the storm, the prophet’s final reaction is to admire God. And the last picture is young people flourishing on grain and new wine: a society with a future, exactly what a struggling remnant needed to be promised.

Uncertain wording. “Tread down the sling stones” (v. 15) probably means the enemy’s missiles are trampled as useless, though some translate “overcome with sling stones”. And verse 17 says only “his” (or “its”) goodness and beauty: God’s, as the ESV takes it, or the people’s, as some translations have it. Either way, the people’s beauty reflects their God’s.

9.title: Behold, Your King Is Coming
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1 to 8 ended with people from every nation taking hold of a Jew’s robe because God is with his people (8:23). Now the first of the book’s two closing oracles begins (chapters 9 to 11), with no dates or visions, looking far beyond Zechariah’s own day (see the introduction).

The message. God is coming to his people as their King, and nothing on earth can stop him. He humbles the proud powers on Judah’s borders and even turns old enemies into family; then the King himself arrives, not on a war horse but on a donkey, righteous, bringing salvation and speaking peace to the nations. Because of the blood of the covenant he frees his captive people, fights for them and treasures them like the jewels of a crown.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were a tiny province with no king, surrounded by richer and stronger neighbours (see the introduction). They needed to know whether David’s throne would stay empty and whether God could protect them, and this chapter answers that their King is on his way.

How the chapter makes its case. First the LORD clears the road (vv. 1–8): judgment moves down from Syria through wealthy Tyre to the Philistine cities, yet Philistia becomes “a remnant for our God”, and God camps at his house as its guard. Then the King comes (vv. 9–10), humble on a donkey, disarming even his own people and speaking peace to the ends of the earth. Then the prisoners go free (vv. 11–13): because of the blood of the covenant, “prisoners of hope” are released and promised double, and God takes up his people as his weapons. Finally the LORD appears as warrior and shepherd (vv. 14–17), saving his flock and making it shine, and the chapter ends in worship: “how great is his goodness”.

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise above all. Matthew and John saw verse 9 fulfilled when Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a colt (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15), the King who came humble because he came to die. By covenant too: “the blood of my covenant” (v. 11) looks ahead to the cup Jesus gave his disciples, “my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). And the King who speaks peace to the nations is the one who “came and preached peace to you who were far off” (Ephesians 2:17).

For us. Our King does not come to take our side in our quarrels but to make peace with God at his own cost, and then peace between enemies. If you feel trapped in a pit you cannot climb out of, you are a prisoner of hope, because Christ’s blood has secured your release. And people he has rescued can lay down their own chariots, trusting him rather than force, money or cleverness.
9.theology:
Wealth and cleverness are no defence against God, yet he does not only defeat his enemies: he converts them and adopts them into his people, and he stands guard over his house himself (vv. 2-8).

The promised king comes to his people righteous, bringing salvation, and humble, as Jesus did when he rode into Jerusalem (v. 9). He disarms his own people and rules the world by speaking peace (v. 10). Prisoners are set free by the blood of God's covenant, which Christ named at the last supper (v. 11; Exod 24:8; Matt 26:28), and believers live as prisoners of hope until God's double restoration comes (v. 12; Isa 61:7). He saves his people as a flock and displays them as the jewels of his crown (v. 16).
9.examples: An island fortress with silver heaped like dust is burned to the ground, while old enemies are absorbed into God's family like an ordinary clan. A world king arrives on a borrowed farm animal, and God's own chariots and war horses are scrapped as unnecessary. A dry cistern with no way out has its door opened by blood; its prisoners still have hope because a promise has been made; and God wears his people like the jewels of a crown.

keyVerse.quote: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
keyVerse.note: This is the centre of the chapter and one of the best-known prophecies in the Old Testament. The King promised to a people without a king comes to them, righteous and bringing salvation, but humble, on a donkey rather than a war horse. Jesus fulfilled it deliberately when he rode into Jerusalem to die (Matthew 21:5).

9.reflection:
Zion is told to rejoice because her King is coming “to you” (v. 9). Why does it matter that the King comes to us rather than summoning us to climb up to him? What does Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem on a donkey show about the kind of King he is?

The first weapons the King breaks are his own people’s (v. 10). Where are you tempted to enlist God on your side of a quarrel, and what would it look like to let Christ’s peace end it instead?

Philistia, Israel’s old enemy, becomes “like a clan in Judah” (v. 7). Who seems to you beyond the reach of the gospel, and how does this promise change the way you pray for them?

“Prisoners of hope” are set free “because of the blood of my covenant” (vv. 11–12). How does the cup of the Lord’s Supper (Matthew 26:28) give hope to someone who feels stuck in a pit they cannot climb out of?

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain, from the LORD who makes the storm clouds, and he will give them showers of rain, to everyone the vegetation in the field.<sup>2</sup>For the household gods utter nonsense, and the diviners see lies; they tell false dreams and give empty consolation. Therefore the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd.<sup>3</sup>"My anger is hot against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders; for the LORD of hosts cares for his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his majestic steed in battle.<sup>4</sup>From him shall come the cornerstone, from him the tent peg, from him the battle bow, from him every ruler— all of them together.<sup>5</sup>They shall be like mighty men in battle, trampling the foe in the mud of the streets; they shall fight because the LORD is with them, and they shall put to shame the riders on horses.<sup>6</sup>"I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph. I will bring them back because I have compassion on them, and they shall be as though I had not rejected them, for I am the LORD their God and I will answer them.<sup>7</sup>Then Ephraim shall become like a mighty warrior, and their hearts shall be glad as with wine. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people need the LORD as their shepherd, not the substitutes they had trusted or the leaders who failed them. They are to ask rain from the LORD who makes the storm clouds (v. 1), because household gods and diviners give only lies and “empty consolation”, and trusting them left the people wandering like sheep without a shepherd (v. 2). So God’s anger burns against the shepherds, “for the LORD of hosts cares for his flock”, and he will turn his frightened sheep into his majestic steed in battle (v. 3). From Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg, the battle bow and every ruler (v. 4), and the flock will triumph “because the LORD is with them” (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: People who will not ask God for rain end up consulting anything, and God holds their leaders responsible.

verseByVerse.quote: Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain, from the LORD who makes the storm clouds, and he will give them showers of rain, to everyone the vegetation in the field. For the household gods utter nonsense, and the diviners see lies; they tell false dreams and give empty consolation. Therefore the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd. "My anger is hot against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders; for the LORD of hosts cares for his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his majestic steed in battle. From him shall come the cornerstone, from him the tent peg, from him the battle bow, from him every ruler— all of them together. They shall be like mighty men in battle, trampling the foe in the mud of the streets; they shall fight because the LORD is with them, and they shall put to shame the riders on horses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ask the LORD, not the substitutes that give empty comfort; God is angry with the leaders who failed his flock, and will make it strong with leaders from Judah and his own presence.

Ask rain from the LORD. A farming community lived or died by the spring rain that filled out the grain before harvest, and in Zechariah’s day the harvests had been failing (Haggai 1:10–11). The temptation was to secure it by the neighbours’ charms and fertility rites. God’s instruction is startlingly simple: ask him, because he is “the LORD who makes the storm clouds”. The alternative to superstition is not self-reliance; it is prayer.

How do I ask? Ask for the plain things. The rent, a job, a test result: nothing is too everyday for the God who makes the clouds, and Jesus taught us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). Ask first. Make prayer the first move, not the last resort. Notice your household gods. What do you quietly trust to make things come right: luck, the market, a contact, your own cleverness? Then do your work as someone who has asked. Keep asking. Farmers asked every spring; we ask every day, and boldly, because of what God has already given: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

The household gods utter nonsense. Household gods (teraphim) were small figures kept for luck and guidance, like those Rachel stole from her father (Genesis 31:19). The verdict on every substitute for God: nonsense, lies, false dreams, “empty consolation”. The horoscope, the charm and the confident guru do console, briefly, and the comfort is empty.

The people wander like sheep. The Hebrew can also be read as past: this is why they went off like sheep into exile. When Jesus looked at the crowds he saw exactly this: they were “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). And he did something about it.

My anger is hot against the shepherds. In the Old Testament shepherds are rulers, the leaders who should have fed the flock (compare Ezekiel 34). The ESV notes that the word for “leaders” is literally “the male goats”, the ones who push to the front. And the reason for God’s anger is stated: “the LORD of hosts cares for his flock”. His anger at bad shepherds comes from his love for the sheep.

Like his majestic steed in battle. The frightened flock becomes God’s own war horse: he does not merely pity the weak; he makes them formidable.

From him shall come the cornerstone. Four pictures of leadership, all coming from Judah’s own people rather than from foreign masters. The cornerstone holds a building square; the tent peg is what everything hangs on (God promised to fasten Eliakim “like a peg in a secure place”, Isaiah 22:23); the battle bow defends; the ruler governs.

The cornerstone from Judah. Many Christians see all four met in one person. The New Testament calls Christ the cornerstone in whom the whole building is joined together (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:6), and the ruler from Judah, to whom the sceptre belongs (Genesis 49:10; Hebrews 7:14). The peg and the bow fit him too, though the New Testament does not use those pictures.

Because the LORD is with them. The secret of their strength is in the middle of verse 5. Not better equipment; better company.

Uncertain wording. The repeated “from him” (v. 4) most likely means from Judah, named just before, though some take it as “from the LORD”; either way, the leaders are God’s gift. All four pictures probably describe the rulers God will raise, since “cornerstone” and “peg” are used of leaders elsewhere (Isaiah 19:13; 22:23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — I Will Whistle for Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD will bring all his scattered people home and restore them completely. He will strengthen Judah and save Joseph, the long-lost north, and they will be “as though I had not rejected them” (v. 6), so that they and their children rejoice in him (v. 7). He will whistle for his redeemed like a shepherd and gather them in (v. 8); even in far countries they will remember him and return (v. 9). In a new exodus he brings them from Egypt and Assyria until there is no room for them, humbling those proud powers (vv. 10–11), and makes them “strong in the LORD” to “walk in his name” (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God whistles for his scattered people like a shepherd calling a flock, and they come.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph. I will bring them back because I have compassion on them, and they shall be as though I had not rejected them, for I am the LORD their God and I will answer them. Then Ephraim shall become like a mighty warrior, and their hearts shall be glad as with wine. Their children shall see it and be glad; their hearts shall rejoice in the LORD. "I will whistle for them and gather them in, for I have redeemed them, and they shall be as many as they were before. Though I scattered them among the nations, yet in far countries they shall remember me, and with their children they shall live and return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of sheer compassion God will bring home both halves of his scattered people, restored as if never rejected, whistling for them like a shepherd.

I will save the house of Joseph. Both halves of the divided nation are named: Judah in the south and “Joseph” in the north, the tribes descended from Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh, scattered by Assyria long before. God intends to have them all, and the reason is his own heart: “because I have compassion on them”.

As though I had not rejected them. Not merely tolerated, but restored so completely that the rejection might never have happened. That is what forgiveness in Christ does. The prodigal comes home and is given the robe and the ring, not a place among the hired servants (Luke 15:19–22). And the God who told them to ask (v. 1) promises, “I will answer them”.

Their children shall see it and be glad. Children who see their parents genuinely glad in God are being given something no lesson can supply.

I will whistle for them. A shepherd’s whistle: a sound the flock knows, cutting across distance, and they come. Isaiah had pictured God whistling for distant nations to come and judge his people (Isaiah 5:26); now he whistles to bring his people home. It works “for I have redeemed them”: they are his already, and the whistle is the call of their owner. Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). Every conversion is someone hearing the whistle.

In far countries they shall remember me. God says he himself scattered them, and the word is literally “sowed”: they were scattered like seed, and seed grows (compare Hosea 2:23). The scattering will not be the end. Distance puts no one out of God’s reach.

Where Christians differ. Does the gathering of Joseph promise a future return of the ten northern tribes? Some Christians expect a further, literal return of those tribes to the land. Others see the promise of reunion under one shepherd (Ezekiel 37:15–28) fulfilled in Christ, who gathers one flock from every nation (John 10:16; Ephesians 2:14–16).

This commentary’s view. This commentary reads the promise, with the New Testament, as met in the one flock of Christ, Jews and Gentiles together.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring them home from the land of Egypt, and gather them from Assyria, and I will bring them to the land of Gilead and to Lebanon, till there is no room for them. He shall pass through the sea of troubles and strike down the waves of the sea, and all the depths of the Nile shall be dried up. The pride of Assyria shall be laid low, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart. I will make them strong in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a new exodus God will bring his people home from every land of bondage until there is no room for them, and make them strong to live as his own.

Till there is no room for them. Egypt and Assyria were the two great places of bondage and exile in Israel’s memory. By Zechariah’s day Assyria had long fallen (its capital Nineveh in 612 BC), so the old names stand for every land where God’s people were held (compare Isaiah 11:11, 16). Gilead and Lebanon, northern lands Assyria took first (2 Kings 15:29), will overflow: the happiest sort of problem.

He shall pass through the sea of troubles. The language is deliberately that of the exodus: a sea divided, the Nile dried up, Egypt humbled. God’s past rescues are the pattern of his future ones. The greatest is the one Jesus spoke of on the mountain, the “departure” (in Greek, his exodus) “which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31), by which he leads his people out of slavery to sin.

The Christian life in two phrases. “Strong in the LORD”: the strength is real, and it is not our own; Paul says, “be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10). And “they shall walk in his name”: ordinary daily living, done as people who belong to him and bear his name. A flock with no shepherd at the start of the chapter; a people walking in God’s name at the end. That is the difference a shepherd makes.

Uncertain wording. Verse 11 is compressed. “He” is most likely the LORD going before his people, as at the Red Sea, and “the sea of troubles” renders two words side by side, “the sea, distress”. The picture is clear even where the grammar is not: God leads his people through whatever stands in the way.

10.title: Ask Rain from the LORD
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 announced the humble King and ended with God saving his people “as the flock of his people” (9:16). Chapter 10 continues the same oracle and takes up that picture: a flock misled by false guides and failed leaders, and the LORD who comes to shepherd it himself.

The message. Look to the LORD and not to substitutes, because he alone gives what his people need, and he cares for his flock. He will deal with the leaders who failed them, raise up from Judah the leaders they need, and gather his scattered people home from every land as surely as he once brought them out of Egypt, restoring them so completely that it will be as though he had never rejected them.

Why it was said. Only a fraction of God’s people had come home, the northern tribes had been scattered for two centuries, and the returned community depended on rains and harvests that had been failing (Haggai 1:10–11; see the introduction). It was tempting to hedge their bets with the charms and diviners of their neighbours, and to think the lost tribes were lost for good.

How the chapter makes its case. It starts with rain (vv. 1–2): ask the LORD, because household gods and diviners give only empty comfort, and trusting them is what scattered the flock. Then the shepherds (vv. 3–5): God’s anger burns against the leaders who failed, because he cares for his flock, and he will turn it into his war horse, with the cornerstone, the tent peg, the bow and every ruler coming from Judah. Then the homecoming (vv. 6–12): God will save Judah and Joseph alike, whistle for his redeemed, and bring them from Egypt and Assyria in a new exodus until there is no room for them, strong in the LORD and walking in his name.

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. Jesus saw the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36), the very condition of verse 2, and came as the good shepherd whose voice his sheep hear (John 10:27). The New Testament names him the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:6) and the ruler descended from Judah (Hebrews 7:14). And the great gathering of the scattered is met in him, who brings other sheep in, so that “there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16).

For us. Take ordinary needs to God first, rather than to the household gods we quietly trust. If you have wandered far, God still whistles for his own, and his forgiveness restores so fully that it is as though he had never rejected you. And those who lead in his church should remember whose flock it is.
10.theology:
The alternative to superstition is not self-reliance but asking God; every substitute for him offers empty consolation and leaves people shepherdless (vv. 1-2; Matt 9:36). His anger against bad shepherds flows from his care for the flock, and the leadership he gives comes from among his people, fulfilled in Christ the cornerstone (vv. 3-4; Eph 2:20). Their strength is his presence, not their equipment (v. 5).

He restores so completely that it is as though he had never rejected them (v. 6), and he calls his own like a shepherd whistling for a flock he has already redeemed (v. 8; John 10:27). Exile puts no one beyond his reach; far countries are often where people start remembering him (v. 9).
10.examples: Farmers are tempted to buy rain from a charm instead of asking God, and find its consolation empty by morning. Leaders are called the male goats that push to the front, while a frightened flock is turned into God's own warhorse. Then a shepherd's whistle carries across a long distance, and so many come home that there is no room for them.

keyVerse.quote: I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph. I will bring them back because I have compassion on them, and they shall be as though I had not rejected them, for I am the LORD their God and I will answer them.
keyVerse.note: Here is the heart of the chapter: God brings his whole scattered people home, south and north, for no reason but his own compassion. The restoration is so complete that it is as though he had never rejected them, which is what forgiveness in Christ does for every sinner who comes home.

10.reflection:
God says, “Ask rain from the LORD” (v. 1). What ordinary needs do you tend to handle without asking God, and what “household gods” (luck, money, contacts, your own cleverness) do you quietly trust instead?

God’s anger burns against the shepherds because he “cares for his flock” (v. 3). What does this teach those who lead in the church, the home or at work? How is Jesus the shepherd those leaders failed to be (Matthew 9:36)?

God promises that his people will be “as though I had not rejected them” (v. 6). Do you find it hard to believe God forgives that completely? How does the father’s welcome of the prodigal son (Luke 15:20–24) help?

“Their children shall see it and be glad” (v. 7). What are the children and young people around you learning from watching your joy, or lack of joy, in God?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens in judgment and shows why it comes: a flock exploited by those who should have cared for it. Fire sweeps the land, from the cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan to the thicket of the Jordan, and the shepherds wail and the lions roar over their ruined glory (vv. 1–3). Then God gives the prophet a part to play: “Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter” (v. 4). Its buyers kill without punishment, its sellers bless the LORD for their profits, and its own shepherds have no pity (v. 5). So God will no longer pity the land, but hands its people over to one another and to their king (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: When leaders treat people as merchandise, God hands the people over to what they have chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars! Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen, for the glorious trees are ruined! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the thick forest has been felled! The sound of the wail of the shepherds, for their glory is ruined! The sound of the roar of the lions, for the thicket of the Jordan is ruined! Thus said the LORD my God: "Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter. Those who buy them slaughter them and go unpunished, and those who sell them say, 'Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich,' and their own shepherds have no pity on them. For I will no longer have pity on the inhabitants of this land, declares the LORD. Behold, I will cause each of them to fall into the hand of his neighbor, and each into the hand of his king, and they shall crush the land, and I will deliver none from their hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment sweeps through the whole land because God’s flock has been exploited by those who should have cared for it, and God sets his prophet to shepherd a flock already doomed.

Open your doors, O Lebanon. A forest fire runs from north to south. Great trees are the Bible’s regular picture for great men, and here they come down. The places mark out the whole land: Lebanon in the north, famous for its cedars; Bashan, the high pastureland east of the Jordan, famous for its oaks; and “the thicket of the Jordan”, the dense jungle along the river where lions had their lairs (Jeremiah 49:19). Some Jewish readers took Lebanon as a picture of the temple, built of cedar, and the Talmud records that Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, before AD 70, applied this verse to the temple’s coming destruction.

The sound of the wail of the shepherds. First the shepherds wail, the leaders who have lost their pastures; then the lions roar, the predators who have lost their cover. When judgment comes, careless leaders and those who preyed on the flock are left with nothing.

Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter. Now Zechariah is given a part to play, and it is a terrible one. Prophets often acted out their messages, and this is one of the darkest. For the hearers, back from exile and rebuilding, it was a warning that return did not guarantee blessing: the story that ended in exile could repeat itself if they rejected the shepherd God gave them.

Those who buy them slaughter them. Three groups are named, and all are guilty. The buyers slaughter and “go unpunished”. The sellers thank God for their profits, “Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich”, using religious language over a trade in human lives. And “their own shepherds have no pity on them”.

Piety and exploitation. This combination is one of the ugliest things in the Bible, and common enough to need naming: people still bless God for gains made at others’ cost. Jesus met it in the temple courts, where trade had turned his Father’s house into “a den of robbers” (Matthew 21:13).

I will no longer have pity. God stops protecting them and hands each one over to his neighbour and his king, who will crush the land. Sometimes God’s severest act is to stop shielding people from the consequences of what they prefer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good shepherd is rejected and priced at a slave’s value, and the flock loses God’s favour and its own unity. The prophet tends the doomed flock with two staffs, Favor and Union (v. 7). He removes three shepherds in a month, but the flock detests him, and he gives it up to its fate (vv. 8–9). He breaks Favor, annulling God’s protecting covenant, and the sheep traders understand (vv. 10–11). Asked to name his wages, they weigh out thirty pieces of silver, “the lordly price”, which God tells him to throw to the potter in the house of the LORD (vv. 12–13). Then he breaks Union, the brotherhood between Judah and Israel (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The good shepherd is valued at the price of a slave, and the rejection of him breaks both grace and unity.

verseByVerse.quote: So I became the shepherd of the flock doomed to be slaughtered by the sheep traders. And I took two staffs, one I named Favor, the other I named Union. And I tended the sheep. In one month I destroyed the three shepherds. But I became impatient with them, and they also detested me. So I said, "I will not be your shepherd. What is to die, let it die. What is to be destroyed, let it be destroyed. And let those who are left devour the flesh of one another." And I took my staff Favor, and I broke it, annulling the covenant that I had made with all the peoples. So it was annulled on that day, and the sheep traders, who were watching me, knew that it was the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet acts out God’s faithful care for his flock, but the flock detests him, so he gives them up and breaks the staff called Favor, ending God’s protection.

One I named Favor, the other I named Union. The prophet takes up the job with two shepherd’s staffs, and their names tell us what God had been giving his people. Favor is his grace, the covenant kindness that kept them. Union is the bond that held Judah and Israel together as one people. Then the quiet line: “And I tended the sheep.” He did the work properly.

In one month I destroyed the three shepherds. The good shepherd deals swiftly with bad leaders: three are removed in a single month.

They also detested me. What matters is the relationship. The flock hated the shepherd who was actually caring for them. That sentence casts a long shadow across the Gospels, for Jesus “came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11).

I will not be your shepherd. The shepherd resigns, and the flock turns on itself. A community that rejects God’s care does not become free; it becomes self-consuming.

I took my staff Favor, and I broke it. The staff is snapped. “The covenant that I had made with all the peoples” is most likely God’s restraint on the nations, which had held them back from destroying his people; now that protection is withdrawn.

Uncertain wording. Who the three shepherds are is unknown. Interpreters have suggested kings, priests and prophets, or three particular rulers, and the text does not say; it is wiser to leave it. “One month” probably means a short time.

Textual note. In verses 7 and 11 the ESV follows the Greek Old Testament in reading “the sheep traders”. The standard Hebrew text, followed by the KJV, reads “the poor of the flock”. On that reading it is the afflicted sheep, not the dealers, who recognise God’s word, as the poor so often did when Jesus came.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to them, "If it seems good to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them." And they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver. Then the LORD said to me, "Throw it to the potter"— the lordly price at which I was priced by them. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the LORD, to the potter. Then I broke my second staff Union, annulling the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The flock values its shepherd at thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, and God has the insulting sum thrown to the potter in his house; Matthew sees it fulfilled when Jesus was betrayed for the same price.

Thirty pieces of silver. The shepherd asks to be paid and leaves the amount to them. What he receives is a calculated insult. The law of Moses set thirty shekels as the compensation for a slave gored to death by someone’s ox (Exodus 21:32). That is what they thought his care was worth: the price of a dead slave.

The lordly price at which I was priced by them. The phrase is heavy with sarcasm, and notice who speaks: the LORD himself. The insult paid to his shepherd is an insult to God. The money is thrown away, into the temple, to the potter.

Judas and the potter’s field. Judas agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), then threw the coins into the temple, and the priests used them to buy a potter’s field. Matthew records it as the fulfilment of prophecy (Matthew 27:9–10). Five centuries before, the amount and the fate of the coins were written down. The good shepherd was priced at the going rate for a slave, by the people he came to save.

The price of everything. In Lady Windermere’s Fan Oscar Wilde has a character define a cynic as “a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.” We price time, attention and even people by what they produce, and feel our own worth rise and fall with salary, grades and numbers online. The leaders in Zechariah did the same with God, and decided his care was worth about what a dead slave was worth. We still make that calculation, whether we think God can be paid off with a respectable minimum of religion or is worth nothing at all. The reversal is that the one we priced so low then paid for us, in a currency no market has. We were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Your value is not what the market says, or even what you say. It is what he paid.

Then I broke my second staff Union. Having rejected the shepherd, the flock loses its unity. That is the order: reject Christ, and the bonds between people begin to fail as well.

Why does Matthew name Jeremiah? Matthew attributes the quotation to “Jeremiah the prophet” (Matthew 27:9), though the words are found here. Christians have explained this in several ways: that Matthew blends Zechariah’s words with Jeremiah’s passages about the potter and the field, that he names the scroll of the prophets by Jeremiah, who stood first in one ancient order, or that a copying error entered early. The first is most likely: Matthew joins Zechariah’s words to Jeremiah’s visit to the potter and purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19; 32), and names the greater prophet, as Mark names Isaiah for words drawn from Malachi and Isaiah together (Mark 1:2–3).

Uncertain wording. Why “the potter”? The potters may have worked for the temple, or the phrase may be a proverb for throwing something away as worthless. Some translations read “the treasury”, a Hebrew word differing by one letter. “The potter” is the harder reading, and it is the one Matthew follows.
verseByVerse.note: The Syriac version reads "into the treasury" where the Hebrew has "to the potter"; Matthew follows the potter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having rejected the good shepherd, the flock is given the shepherd it deserves. The prophet takes up “the equipment of a foolish shepherd” (v. 15), picturing a leader God will raise up who neither cares for the perishing, nor seeks the young, nor heals the maimed, nor feeds the healthy, but devours the flock (v. 16). Yet God does not excuse him: “Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock!” The arm that should have defended the sheep will wither, and the eye that should have watched over them will be blinded (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: A people who reject the shepherd God sends will get the shepherd they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Take once more the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For behold, I am raising up in the land a shepherd who does not care for those being destroyed, or seek the young or heal the maimed or nourish the healthy, but devours the flesh of the fat ones, tearing off even their hoofs. "Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! May the sword strike his arm and his right eye! Let his arm be wholly withered, his right eye utterly blinded!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the flock rejected the good shepherd, God gives it a worthless one who devours it, yet he will judge that shepherd for deserting the sheep.

The equipment of a foolish shepherd. A second, worse piece of acting: the prophet must play a bad shepherd.

A shepherd who does not care for those being destroyed. Read the list of what he fails to do: he does not care for the perishing, seek the young, heal the maimed or nourish the healthy. Ezekiel had made the same charge against Israel’s leaders (Ezekiel 34:4). What he does do is eat the best of the flock.

The shepherd they preferred. This is God’s judgment on a people who rejected the shepherd he sent: they get the shepherd they preferred. Leaders are often what a community has asked for.

Woe to my worthless shepherd. The arm that should have defended the sheep is withered, the eye that should have watched them blinded. God does not treat the abuse of the vulnerable lightly, and anyone harmed by a leader who used the flock for himself should know that God sees it and calls it what it is.

Struck, and does not desert. The whole dark chapter leaves us needing a shepherd who is the opposite of this one. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Here the shepherd deserts the flock and is struck; there the Shepherd is struck (13:7) and does not desert. That contrast is the mercy this chapter drives us toward.

Who is the worthless shepherd? Most likely the corrupt leaders God let the people have after they rejected the good shepherd, the rulers of Jesus’ generation; some see a final antichrist figure. Either way, he is judged (v. 17).

11.title: Thirty Pieces of Silver
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 closes the first oracle (chapters 9 to 11). After the bright promises of the coming King and the gathered flock, the mood suddenly darkens: fire runs through the forests, and Zechariah is told to act the part of a shepherd.

The message. The flock the good shepherd came to save rejects him and values him at the price of a slave, and in rejecting him they reject God himself. Judgment follows: the staffs of Favor and Union are broken, the flock is left to the traders, and God hands it over to a worthless shepherd who devours it. Blessing cannot be presumed; to despise the shepherd God sends is to lose everything.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had just heard great promises (chapters 9 and 10) and might have assumed that blessing was now guaranteed. But their fathers had gone into exile for refusing God’s word (1:4–6; 7:11–14; see the introduction), and this chapter warns that the same story could be repeated, as in time it would be, on a scale beyond anything they had known.

How the chapter makes its case. A lament opens it (vv. 1–3): fire sweeps from Lebanon to the Jordan, and the shepherds wail. Then the commission (vv. 4–6): the prophet must shepherd a flock doomed to slaughter, exploited by buyers, by sellers who thank God for their profits, and by pitiless shepherds. Then the drama (vv. 7–14): he tends the flock with two staffs, Favor and Union, but the flock detests him; he breaks Favor, is paid thirty pieces of silver, throws them to the potter in the house of the LORD, and breaks Union. Finally (vv. 15–17) he plays a worthless shepherd, whom God will raise up and then curse.

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise, and in the character of God himself. Matthew saw the thirty pieces of silver, thrown into the temple and used to buy a potter’s field, fulfilled in Judas’s betrayal (Matthew 26:15; 27:3–10). The shepherd the flock detested is the good shepherd who “came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). And it is the LORD who speaks of “the lordly price at which I was priced by them” (v. 13): the one they valued at a slave’s price was God himself, come to shepherd his people.

For us. Christ is not someone we can price at a respectable minimum; he is worth everything, and he ransomed us “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Beware of piety used as cover for gain, and pray for leaders who seek the lost and heal the hurt. And if you have despised his care, come back: the good shepherd still calls.
11.theology:
When leaders treat people as merchandise and bless God for the profits, he sees both the trade and the piety, and his severest judgment can be to stop protecting people from what they have chosen (vv. 5-6). A flock that rejects its shepherd does not become free but self-consuming, and his favour and the unity of his people are gifts that can be withdrawn (vv. 9-14).

The shepherd God sends is valued at the price of a dead slave, as Jesus was in his betrayal (vv. 12-13; Exod 21:32; Matt 26:15; 27:9-10). Those who reject him receive the shepherd they preferred (vv. 15-16; Ezek 34:4), but God curses shepherds who desert and devour the flock, and sends the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for it (v. 17; John 10:11).
11.examples: A forest fire runs the length of a country, and the lions lose their cover. Sellers thank God for the profits of a trade in lives. A shepherd carries two staffs named Favor and Union, and his flock comes to detest him; his wages are weighed out, flung into the temple, and later used to buy a field. The chapter ends with a worthless shepherd's arm withered and his watching eye blinded.

keyVerse.quote: Then I said to them, “If it seems good to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them.” And they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter. The shepherd who has cared for the flock is valued at the price of a dead slave, and the LORD takes the insult as aimed at himself (v. 13). Matthew saw it fulfilled when Jesus was betrayed for the same thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15; 27:9–10).

11.reflection:
The sellers say, “Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich” (v. 5). Where might we use religious language to cover gain at other people’s expense, in business, ministry or family life?

The flock detested the shepherd who was caring for them (v. 8). Why do people resist God’s care, and how did that happen to Jesus (John 1:11)? Are there ways you resist it?

The leaders valued God’s shepherd at thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (vv. 12–13). What price do people put on Christ today, and how does 1 Peter 1:18–19 answer the question of what you are worth?

The worthless shepherd neglects the young, the injured and the weak (v. 16). What would it look like for your church to seek out and care for exactly those people?
