verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Cup of Staggering and a Heavy Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Creator will defend his small, weak people against the whole world, so that no one can boast except in him. The God who stretched out the heavens and formed the human spirit speaks (v. 1). He makes Jerusalem “a cup of staggering” and “a heavy stone for all the peoples”: the nations gather against it, and all who lift it hurt themselves (vv. 2–3). He strikes their horses with panic and their riders with madness, while keeping his eyes open for Judah, whose clans see that the city’s strength is the LORD (vv. 4–5). Judah becomes fire in a woodpile (v. 6), the tents of Judah are saved first so that no one can boast (v. 7), and the feeblest becomes “like David”, the house of David “like God” (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: God makes his besieged people the stone that injures everyone who tries to lift it.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle of the word of the LORD concerning Israel: Thus declares the LORD, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth and formed the spirit of man within him: "Behold, I am about to make Jerusalem a cup of staggering to all the surrounding peoples. The siege of Jerusalem will also be against Judah. On that day I will make Jerusalem a heavy stone for all the peoples. All who lift it will surely hurt themselves. And all the nations of the earth will gather against it. On that day, declares the LORD, I will strike every horse with panic, and its rider with madness. But for the sake of the house of Judah I will keep my eyes open, when I strike every horse of the peoples with blindness. Then the clans of Judah shall say to themselves, 'The inhabitants of Jerusalem have strength through the LORD of hosts, their God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Creator will make small, weak Jerusalem too dangerous for the nations to swallow, defending his people himself so that they learn their strength is in him.

Who stretched out the heavens. The second oracle opens with God’s credentials, and they are cosmic: he stretched out the heavens, founded the earth and “formed the spirit of man within him”. The third is the most personal. The God who made the galaxies also made the inner life of every person, which is why he can pour out a spirit of grace in verse 10 and change how people see.

A cup of staggering. Two images for what God will make of a small, vulnerable city. A cup of staggering: the nations drink it down and cannot walk straight. And a heavy stone: the kind of boulder men tried to lift to prove their strength, which ruins the back of everyone who tries. For the first hearers this was a remarkable promise. Jerusalem was small and poor, its walls in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them, its neighbours opposed to the rebuilding (Ezra 4:1–5; Nehemiah 4:1–8). Their safety would never lie in numbers or walls, but in God (compare 2:4–5).

The cup of God’s wrath. Elsewhere the “cup of staggering” is the cup of God’s wrath (Isaiah 51:17, 22). On the night before he died, Jesus prayed that this cup might pass from him, and then drank it (Matthew 26:39), so that his people would never have to.

All who lift it will surely hurt themselves. The story of God’s people is littered with powers that lifted the stone and hurt themselves.

I will strike every horse with panic. The enemy’s cavalry is disabled from inside: panic in the horses, madness in the riders, blindness in the whole force. Meanwhile God says, “I will keep my eyes open” for his people. And the clans of Judah, the country people, draw the right conclusion: the city’s strength is not its walls but “the LORD of hosts, their God”.

Where Christians differ. When does this siege of Jerusalem happen? Dispensational Christians, who expect the promises to Israel to be fulfilled literally in the land, look for a siege of the modern city before Christ returns. Others take Jerusalem to stand for God’s people, assaulted by the world throughout this age and finally at its end (Revelation 20:8–9), and rescued by God himself.

This commentary’s view. This commentary takes the second reading as the likelier, since the New Testament says believers have already come to “the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). Faithful Christians differ here, and all agree that God rescues his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day I will make the clans of Judah like a blazing pot in the midst of wood, like a flaming torch among sheaves. And they shall devour to the right and to the left all the surrounding peoples, while Jerusalem shall again be inhabited in its place, in Jerusalem. "And the LORD will give salvation to the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not surpass that of Judah. On that day the LORD will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the feeblest among them on that day shall be like David, and the house of David shall be like God, like the angel of the LORD, going before them. And on that day I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will make his small people a consuming fire to their enemies, save the humble first so that no one can boast, and make the weakest as strong as David and David’s house like God himself.

Like a blazing pot in the midst of wood. Two pictures of small things with enormous effect: a pot of burning coals set down in a woodpile, and a flaming torch dropped among dry sheaves at harvest. Judah’s clans are not numerous; they do not need to be.

Salvation to the tents of Judah first. A revealing detail. God deliberately saves the country people in their tents first, so that the capital and the royal family cannot claim the credit. God arranges his rescues so that the proud cannot become prouder.

The feeblest among them. Now the promise rises. The feeblest, the one who stumbles, the one everyone helps, “shall be like David”, the giant-killer. And the royal house will be “like God, like the angel of the LORD, going before them”, as the angel once went before Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 14:19).

Fully true of only one son of David. That language is so exalted that it can be fully true of only one son of David: Jesus, who is both David’s descendant and God. This commentary takes the angel of the LORD to be the Son before his incarnation (see the introduction); when the Son became David’s son, David’s house really did go before God’s people as God himself. In him the weakest believer is made strong (2 Corinthians 12:9).

I will seek to destroy all the nations. God’s commitment to defend his people is total. But what he does next, in his people’s own hearts, is more wonderful still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — A Spirit of Grace and Mourning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s greatest rescue happens inside his people: he gives them grace to see the one they pierced and to grieve. He pours out “a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy”, so that when they look “on me, on him whom they have pierced”, they mourn as for an only child (v. 10). The grief is as great as the nation’s mourning at Megiddo (v. 11). And it is deeply personal: the royal and priestly families and all the rest mourn each by itself, and their wives by themselves (vv. 12–14), on the very day a fountain is opened to cleanse them (13:1).
verseByVerse.theology: God pours out grace that makes his people look at the one they pierced and grieve, and that grief is the beginning of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child, and weep bitterly over him, as one weeps over a firstborn. On that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will pour out his Spirit so that his people look on the one they pierced, who is somehow God himself, and mourn for him with the bitter grief of true repentance; John saw it fulfilled at the cross.

A spirit of grace and pleas for mercy. The verse gives three things in order. First, what God gives. Before anyone looks or mourns, God pours out the Spirit who makes them want mercy. Repentance is not something people work up; it is a gift. When the crowd at Pentecost “were cut to the heart” and asked what they should do (Acts 2:37), that was this verse happening.

When they look on me, on him whom they have pierced. Second, what they see. The pronoun shifts within a single line: God says “look on me”, and then at once “him whom they have pierced”. The one pierced is somehow both God himself and another. The Old Testament does not explain it; it simply says it, and leaves the sentence standing for five hundred years.

Fulfilled at the cross. John saw the explanation with his own eyes. When a soldier put a spear into Jesus’ side, he wrote: “And again another Scripture says, ‘They will look on him whom they have pierced’” (John 19:37). Revelation applies the same verse to Christ’s return: “every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7). The riddle is answered in him: the Word who was God became flesh (John 1:1, 14), so that God the Son could be pierced.

They shall mourn for him. Third, what they do: they mourn “as one mourns for an only child”. Not the mourning of despair but of love and shame together, the grief of realising what we have done to someone who loved us. That is what true repentance feels like when the cross comes into focus.

Isn’t God far above our pain? Many thoughtful people assume that if there is a God, he must be serene and untouchable, watching human suffering from a great height. The sceptic is right to find that god hard to love: a God who never bled seems to have little to say to a hospital ward or a mass grave. Zechariah’s sentence breaks the picture open. The LORD who stretched out the heavens (v. 1) says his people will look on him whom they have pierced. John Stott wrote in The Cross of Christ that he could never himself believe in God if it were not for the cross, and asked, “In the real world of pain, how could one worship a God who was immune to it?” The cross does not explain every sorrow (see the note on Job 38:1–4). It does something better: it shows that God has not stood off from our wounds but taken them into himself, and they were wounds we made. That is why this mourning is not despair. You cannot grieve this deeply over someone until you have begun to see how much he loved you.

Where Christians differ. When does this happen? Many in the Reformed tradition see it fulfilled from Pentecost onwards, whenever Jews or Gentiles look to the crucified Christ and grieve over their sin. Many others, including many Reformed readers of Romans 11, expect in addition a future turning of the Jewish people to their Messiah, when “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26). Both agree on what the verse describes: God’s Spirit poured out, a pierced Saviour looked at, and hearts broken and healed.

This commentary’s view. The first is the surer reading of this verse, since John applies it to the cross; if such a future turning comes, as this commentary with humility expects, it will be many more people looking on the same pierced Saviour.

How Jewish readers take it. Many Jewish interpreters read the verse as the people turning to God in grief over Israelites slain by their enemies, the pierced one being distinct from the speaker. Yet the Talmud (Sukkah 52a) records the view that this mourning is for the Messiah son of Joseph, who would be killed, so some rabbinic tradition also heard here a slain Messiah mourned by Israel. This commentary follows John (John 19:37), and looks with hope for the day when many in Israel look on him with this same grief and grace (Romans 11:26).

Uncertain wording. Hadad-rimmon is named nowhere else. It is probably a place near Megiddo, where the nation mourned King Josiah, killed in battle there (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:24–25); some think instead of mourning rites for the pagan storm god Hadad, also called Rimmon. Either way, this grief will be on a national scale, and for the right person.

Textual note. Nearly all Hebrew manuscripts read “on me”; a few read “on him”, as John quotes it. “Me” is the harder and better-attested reading, and the KJV and ESV both keep it. Some translations render it “look to me concerning him whom they pierced”, which separates the two, but the plainer sense is that the people look on God himself, pierced.
verseByVerse.note: Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo is linked with mourning for King Josiah, killed there.

verseByVerse.quote: The land shall mourn, each family by itself: the family of the house of David by itself, and their wives by themselves; the family of the house of Nathan by itself, and their wives by themselves; the family of the house of Levi by itself, and their wives by themselves; the family of the Shimeites by itself, and their wives by themselves; and all the families that are left, each by itself, and their wives by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mourning reaches every family, from the royal and priestly houses down, and each person grieves alone, because no one repents by association.

Four families named. The mourning is described with great care (the ESV notes that “family” may be “clan” throughout). Four families are named: the royal house of David and the line of Nathan (probably David’s son, 2 Samuel 5:14, through whom Luke traces Jesus’ descent, Luke 3:31), and the priestly house of Levi and the line of the Shimeites (from Levi’s grandson Shimei, Numbers 3:17–18). Kings and priests, the two leading orders, and then “all the families that are left”.

Each by itself. The phrase repeats: each family by itself, and their wives by themselves. Nobody mourns in a crowd; even husbands and wives grieve apart.

Personal repentance. This repentance is not a public ceremony people attend. Each household, and each person within it, has to look at the pierced one alone. A person can be carried a long way on the faith of a family or a church, but nobody repents by association. At some point each of us is alone with what we have done and with the one we did it to. And the promise of the next verse is that on exactly that day a fountain is opened.

12.title: They Shall Look on Me Whom They Have Pierced
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 opens the book’s second oracle (chapters 12 to 14). The first ended with the good shepherd rejected and sold for thirty pieces of silver (chapter 11); this one shows what God will do for the people who rejected him.

The message. God will defend his people against the whole world and, more wonderfully still, change their hearts. Small, weak Jerusalem becomes a cup that makes the nations stagger and a stone that injures all who try to lift it, because the LORD fights for her and makes the feeblest like David. Then God pours out a spirit of grace, and his people look on the one they pierced, who is somehow God himself, and mourn for him with a grief that leads to cleansing (13:1).

Why it was said. Jerusalem in Zechariah’s day was small and poor, its walls still broken and its neighbours hostile (see the introduction). The people needed to know that their safety lay in God and not in walls, and that God would deal not only with their enemies but with their own sin.

How the chapter makes its case. First the God who made heaven, earth and the human spirit speaks (v. 1). He makes Jerusalem a cup of staggering and a heavy stone for the nations that gather against it, striking their horses with panic while keeping his eyes on Judah (vv. 2–5). He makes Judah’s clans like fire in a woodpile, saves the country tents first so that no one can boast, and makes the feeblest like David and David’s house like God (vv. 6–9). Then comes the deeper rescue (vv. 10–14): God pours out a spirit of grace, and the people look on him whom they pierced and mourn, as great a mourning as the nation ever knew, family by family and each one alone.

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise, and in the character of God revealed in him. John saw verse 10 fulfilled when a soldier’s spear pierced Jesus’ side: “They will look on him whom they have pierced” (John 19:37); and Revelation looks to its completion, when “every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7). The LORD says “look on me”: in Christ, God the Son took flesh so that God himself could be pierced for his people. And a house of David that is “like God” (v. 8) is fully true only of Jesus, David’s son and God’s Son.

For us. Repentance is God’s gift before it is our act, so ask him for the spirit of grace, for yourself and for others. Look long at the one we pierced, and let grief over what our sin cost him lead each of us, personally, to the fountain he has opened. And when the world seems to close in on the church, remember who has made it a stone too heavy to lift.
12.theology:
The God who made the heavens also formed the human spirit, and can therefore change how people see (v. 1). He makes a vulnerable people the stone that injures everyone who lifts it, disabling his enemies while keeping watch over his own (vv. 2-4). He arranges his rescues so that the proud cannot take the credit, and in his hands the feeblest believer is made like David (vv. 7-8).

Repentance begins with God pouring out a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy; it is a gift, not an achievement (v. 10; Acts 2:37). The one pierced is both God and another, as the cross revealed (v. 10; Rev 1:7), and true mourning over sin is personal: no one repents by association (vv. 12-14).
12.examples: A city that looks easy to take ruins the back of everyone who lifts it, and its enemies' cavalry is disabled by panic rather than by weapons. Judah is a pot of coals set down in a woodpile, the villages are saved first so the capital cannot boast, and the feeblest man in the city fights like David. Then a single line says both “look on me” and “him whom they have pierced”, and families grieve in separate rooms, husbands and wives apart.

keyVerse.quote: And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child, and weep bitterly over him, as one weeps over a firstborn.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the chapter and one of the most astonishing verses in the Old Testament. God gives the grace to repent, and the one his people look on is both God himself and one who has been pierced. John saw it fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37), where God the Son was pierced for the people who pierced him.

12.reflection:
God introduces himself as the one who “formed the spirit of man within him” (v. 1), and then pours out “a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy” (v. 10). Why does real repentance have to begin with God’s work in us, and how should that shape the way we pray for people who seem far from him?

God saves “the tents of Judah first” so that no one can boast (v. 7). Where are you tempted to take credit for what God has done, in your church or your own life?

“When they look on me, on him whom they have pierced” (v. 10): John saw this at the cross (John 19:37). What does it mean to you that the one pierced is God himself? How does that answer the charge that God is far above our pain?

Each family mourns “by itself, and their wives by themselves” (v. 12). Why can no one repent by association? Have you yourself looked at the pierced one and come to the fountain he has opened (13:1)?

13.text: <sup>1</sup>"On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness.<sup>2</sup>"And on that day, declares the LORD of hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, so that they shall be remembered no more. And also I will remove from the land the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness.<sup>3</sup>And if anyone again prophesies, his father and mother who bore him will say to him, 'You shall not live, for you speak lies in the name of the LORD.' And his father and mother who bore him shall pierce him through when he prophesies.<sup>4</sup>"On that day every prophet will be ashamed of his vision when he prophesies. He will not put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive,<sup>5</sup>but he will say, 'I am no prophet, I am a worker of the soil, for a man sold me in my youth.'<sup>6</sup>And if one asks him, 'What are these wounds on your back?' he will say, 'The wounds I received in the house of my friends.'<sup>7</sup>"Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me," declares the LORD of hosts. "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; I will turn my hand against the little ones.<sup>8</sup>In the whole land, declares the LORD, two thirds shall be cut off and perish, and one third shall be left alive.<sup>9</sup>And I will put this third into the fire, and refine them as one refines silver, and test them as gold is tested. They will call upon my name, and I will answer them. I will say, 'They are my people'; and they will say, 'The LORD is my God.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Fountain for Sin and Uncleanness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s cleansing of his people is complete: he washes away their guilt and removes everything that defiled them. A fountain is opened for the royal family and the ordinary citizen alike, to cleanse them “from sin and uncleanness” (v. 1). Then God roots out the sources of the dirt: the idols, down to their very names, the lying prophets and “the spirit of uncleanness” (v. 2). False prophecy becomes so abhorrent that a prophet’s own parents will not shelter him (v. 3), and the prophets themselves, ashamed, throw off the hairy cloak, deny they were ever prophets and explain away their scars (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's cleansing is a fountain that never runs dry, and it is matched by the removal of everything false.

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness. "And on that day, declares the LORD of hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, so that they shall be remembered no more. And also I will remove from the land the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness. And if anyone again prophesies, his father and mother who bore him will say to him, 'You shall not live, for you speak lies in the name of the LORD.' And his father and mother who bore him shall pierce him through when he prophesies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers his people’s mourning with a fountain that washes their sin away, and he clears out the idols and lying prophets that defiled them.

On that day. Chapter 12 ended with every family mourning over the one they had pierced (12:10–14). This is God’s answer to that grief, on the same day.

A fountain opened. A fountain, not a basin: a basin gets dirty and must be refilled; a fountain keeps flowing. And it is “opened”: it was not open before, and someone opened it.

For the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The royal family of David and the ordinary citizens: one fountain for the palace and the back street.

To cleanse them from sin and uncleanness. Under the law, sacrifices for sin and washings for uncleanness had to be repeated endlessly; the word for uncleanness is the one in the “water for impurity” of Numbers 19:9. Here both are dealt with by one open source.

I will cut off the names of the idols. Cleansing has two sides: the fountain washes, and God removes the sources of the dirt, the idols down to their very names (compare Hosea 2:17), the lying “prophets” and “the spirit of uncleanness” that moved them. So God changes the person, not only the record: not only pardon but a new life, what the New Testament calls “the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

The prophets. The danger was real in Judah after the exile. A generation or two later Nehemiah had to face prophets hired to frighten him, among them the prophetess Noadiah (Nehemiah 6:10–14).

His father and mother who bore him. The law required death for a false prophet (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20), and would not let even a close relative who enticed others to idolatry be shielded (Deuteronomy 13:6–10). The shock is that his own parents act, and “pierce him through” is the verb used in 12:10: a people that once pierced the true one will no longer shelter a false one.

What it does not mean. We are not told to imitate this. We live under Christ, who rebuked his disciples for wanting to call down fire (Luke 9:54–55), and the church’s discipline is the word and, at most, exclusion from its fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:13), never the sword. The point is how seriously God takes lying in his name.

Where the fountain is. Christians know where it was opened. Just before quoting 12:10, John records blood and water flowing from Christ’s pierced side (John 19:34–37). His blood can “purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14), and “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

Why can’t we wash our own hands? We are told that guilt is a feeling to be managed and sin an old-fashioned word. Yet much of life is still about being clean: we detox our diets, scrub our histories online, and are quick to name what is unclean in others and slow to bear it in ourselves. The word has gone; the stain has stayed. Shakespeare saw it in Macbeth, staring at his hands after the murder: “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” Religion offers to wash us by effort, the secular world by distraction or self-acceptance, but both are basins, refilled daily and always dirty. Zechariah promises a fountain opened by someone else. The cleansing is not something we do to ourselves; it was done to Christ, whose side was opened, so that “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day every prophet will be ashamed of his vision when he prophesies. He will not put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive, but he will say, 'I am no prophet, I am a worker of the soil, for a man sold me in my youth.' And if one asks him, 'What are these wounds on your back?' he will say, 'The wounds I received in the house of my friends.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
False prophets will be so discredited that they disown their own trade, throwing off the prophet’s cloak and explaining away their scars.

He will not put on a hairy cloak. Every prophet will be ashamed of his vision, because lying visions will impress no one. The hairy cloak, the garment Elijah wore (2 Kings 1:8), was the prophet’s recognised uniform; these men had worn it as a disguise, “in order to deceive”. Now it is abandoned because the trade is discredited.

I am no prophet, I am a worker of the soil. The denial is total: he claims to have worked the land since boyhood. Amos had said almost the same words honestly, “I was no prophet”, but a herdsman whom God took from following the flock (Amos 7:14–15). Amos said it because it was true and God had called him anyway; this man says it to escape.

What are these wounds on your back? Someone spots the scars. The likely background is the practice of pagan prophets who cut themselves in their frenzy, as the prophets of Baal did on Carmel (1 Kings 18:28). Caught out, the man invents a story about a scuffle at a friend’s house.

Religious costume today. It is still possible to wear the uniform of spirituality (the vocabulary, the manner, the confident tone) while selling a lie (Matthew 7:15). When we ourselves are found out, the cleansed response is not a cover story but the fountain of verse 1.

Where Christians differ. “The wounds I received in the house of my friends” is often quoted of Christ, who was indeed wounded by his own people.

This commentary’s view. In context the speaker is a false prophet covering his tracks, so it is better to take the words as they stand. The striking of Jesus comes in the very next verse, and there the reference to him is unmistakable.

Uncertain wording. In verse 5, “for a man sold me in my youth” may also be read, as the ESV notes, “for the land has been my possession since my youth”; either way he claims to have been a farmer all his life. In verse 6, the ESV notes that the Hebrew is “wounds between your hands”, which may mean wounds on the chest or back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cleansing costs God his own shepherd. The LORD summons his sword against “the man who stands next to me”, and when the shepherd is struck the sheep are scattered (v. 7), the very words Jesus applied to his arrest. A great sifting follows, two thirds cut off and one third left (v. 8), and even that third goes through the fire, refined like silver and tested like gold (v. 9). But the fire has a goal: a people who call on God and are answered, and the covenant spoken from both sides, “They are my people” and “The LORD is my God.”
verseByVerse.theology: God's own sword falls on his shepherd, and out of the scattering he refines a people who are truly his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me," declares the LORD of hosts. "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; I will turn my hand against the little ones. In the whole land, declares the LORD, two thirds shall be cut off and perish, and one third shall be left alive. And I will put this third into the fire, and refine them as one refines silver, and test them as gold is tested. They will call upon my name, and I will answer them. I will say, 'They are my people'; and they will say, 'The LORD is my God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons his own sword against his shepherd, the one who stands beside him as his equal, and through the scattering and refining that follow he makes a people who truly belong to him.

Awake, O sword, against my shepherd. Now the chapter turns, and the sword is God’s own. Chapter 11 cursed a worthless shepherd (11:17); this one is “my shepherd”.

The man who stands next to me. The Hebrew word, found elsewhere only in Leviticus, means a fellow or neighbour, one who stands on the same level. The phrase sets this shepherd side by side with God himself.

Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. When the shepherd falls, nothing holds the flock together, and the little ones share its suffering (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Two thirds shall be cut off. The terrible numbers are not a forecast of exact figures; they picture a thorough sifting, and they are meant to sober us. Even the surviving third is not left as it is: it goes “into the fire”.

Refine them as one refines silver. Refining is not punishment. A silversmith heats the metal to bring the impurities to the surface so that he can lift them off. Malachi uses the same picture of the Lord’s coming (Malachi 3:3).

They are my people. It ends in the covenant promise that runs through the whole Bible (Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 31:33; Revelation 21:3): “They are my people”, and “The LORD is my God.” Two sentences, one from each side, and that is what all the striking and refining was for.

Strike the shepherd: Jesus’ own reading. Walking out to the garden on the night he was betrayed, Jesus told his disciples: “You will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered’” (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27). He knew the verse was about himself, and who wielded the sword. It was not Rome or the Sanhedrin: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10).

Struck in our place. That is the heart of the gospel. Only the one who stands beside God could bear God’s sword for the flock, and he was struck in the place of the sheep. Even the scattering of the disciples was foretold and forgiven: scattered that night, they were gathered by the risen Shepherd, who had promised, “after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee” (Matthew 26:32).

In the furnace. When a believer is in the furnace of suffering, the question is not “has God abandoned me?” but “what is he doing?” Sometimes he is lifting off impurity; sometimes he is proving “the tested genuineness of your faith”, which Peter calls “more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire” (1 Peter 1:7). Not every fire answers to a particular sin, but no fire is wasted.

What it means to call on his name. “They will call upon my name” comes straight after the fire. It is the cry of people still warm from the furnace, not a calm-day exercise. To call on someone’s name is to appeal to them by who they are, the way a child shouts for a parent in the night: a claim on someone who has bound himself to you. And God speaks first: “I will answer them” is promised before we hear a word of theirs. Timothy Keller often pointed out that prayer continues a conversation God has already begun through his word and his grace. The name we call on now is Jesus: Paul applies Joel’s matching promise (Joel 2:32) to him, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). Because the Shepherd was struck, we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). So do not wait until you feel calm or worthy before you pray. See Prayer in the Theological Dictionary.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters have usually taken the struck shepherd as a human leader, often linked with the worthless shepherd of 11:17 or with a ruler struck in judgment, and not as the Messiah. They read the refined third as the faithful remnant of Israel, brought through the fire into covenant with God, and that hope both readings share. This commentary reads the shepherd as Jesus, who applied the verse to himself (Matthew 26:31), and the remnant as those gathered by the Shepherd struck in their place.

Uncertain wording. “I will turn my hand against the little ones” can be read two ways. The same Hebrew phrase describes judgment that purifies, “I will turn my hand against you and will smelt away your dross” (Isaiah 1:25), and that is the likelier sense: the little ones share the flock’s suffering, which fits the refining of verses 8–9. Some read it instead as God turning his hand to protect them.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quoted v. 7 on the night he was arrested.

13.title: A Fountain Opened
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 runs straight on in the book’s second oracle (chapters 12–14). Chapter 12 ended with Jerusalem rescued from the nations and every family mourning bitterly as they looked “on him whom they have pierced” (12:10); this chapter tells what God does for those mourners “on that day”.

The message. God answers repentant grief with cleansing. He opens a fountain that washes away sin and uncleanness, and he roots out the idols and lying prophets that had defiled his people. But the cleansing will cost him dearly: he turns his own sword on his shepherd, the man who stands beside him, and through the scattering and refining that follow he makes a people who truly call him their God.

Why it was said. Idolatry and false prophecy were exactly what had brought Judah into exile, and the returned exiles had been warned not to be like their fathers (1:4). Within a generation prophets for hire were troubling Jerusalem again (Nehemiah 6:10–14; see the introduction). The people needed to know whether God could make them clean for good, and at what cost.

How the chapter makes its case. First the fountain (v. 1): a cleansing that never runs dry, open to the royal family and the ordinary citizen alike. Then its fruit (vv. 2–6): idols forgotten, and false prophecy so discredited that parents will not shelter it and prophets disown their trade. Then its cost (vv. 7–9): God’s sword wakes against his own shepherd, the flock is scattered, and through a fire that refines rather than destroys a remnant emerges to speak the covenant’s two sentences, “They are my people” and “The LORD is my God.”

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise, which Jesus himself claimed. On the night of his arrest he quoted verse 7 and told his disciples they would all fall away (Matthew 26:31). So the shepherd struck by God’s sword is the Son, and “the man who stands next to me” reveals God’s own equal coming to bear the blow. The fountain was opened when his pierced side poured out blood and water (John 19:34), and “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

For us. No stain is beyond this fountain, and no one has to wash himself before coming to it: it was opened by another, at the cost of his life. Come to it daily, not only once. And when the fire comes, remember that the Refiner is lifting off dross, not throwing away silver, and that his last word over those he refines is “my people”.
13.theology:
God's answer to repentant mourning is a fountain that is opened and never runs dry (v. 1; Heb 9:14; 1 John 1:7). Cleansing has two sides, sin forgiven and the sources of defilement removed (v. 2; Titus 3:5), and in a cleansed community lying in God's name is treated with the utmost seriousness and its religious costume stripped away (vv. 3-4).

God himself summons the sword against his own shepherd, the man who stands next to him, and Jesus applied the verse to his own arrest (v. 7; Mark 14:27). God then refines the remnant in fire to remove impurities, not to destroy them (v. 9; Mal 3:3; 1 Pet 1:7), and the goal of it all is the covenant exchange: "They are my people" and "The LORD is my God" (v. 9).
13.examples: A fountain rather than a basin is opened for the palace and the back street alike. A prophet's hairy cloak is abandoned because the trade is discredited, and a man invents a story to explain his scars. Then a sword is summoned by God against God's own shepherd, a silversmith heats metal to lift the impurities off the surface, and two short sentences are spoken, one from each side of a covenant.

keyVerse.quote: On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness.
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to the mourning over the pierced one in 12:10, and the heart of the chapter: a cleansing opened by God himself that never runs dry, for king and commoner alike. The rest of the chapter shows its fruit, a people freed from idols and lies, and its cost, the shepherd struck by God’s own sword (v. 7). Christians know where it was opened: at the cross, where Christ’s pierced side poured out blood and water (John 19:34).

13.reflection:
The fountain in verse 1 is opened for people who have just mourned over the one they pierced (12:10). Why does real cleansing begin with seeing what our sin did to Christ? What “basins” do people around you use to try to feel clean?

In verses 2–6 cleansing means not only pardon but the removal of idols and lies, even when family loyalty is at stake. What idol or comfortable falsehood might God want to cut off from your life or your church?

Jesus applied verse 7 to himself on the night he was arrested (Matthew 26:31). What difference does it make that the sword that struck the shepherd was God’s own, and that it fell on him instead of the flock?

Verse 9 pictures suffering as a refiner’s fire that ends in “They are my people” and “The LORD is my God.” How have you seen God use hard times to refine faith? How can we help a suffering friend without suggesting that every trial is a punishment?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — His Feet on the Mount of Olives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God lets his people come to the very edge of ruin, and then comes himself to rescue them. The day of the LORD opens with Jerusalem taken, plundered and half its people exiled, for God gathers the nations against it, though a remnant is not cut off (vv. 1–2). Then the LORD goes out to fight those nations (v. 3). His feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits from east to west to open a valley of escape, and his people flee as their ancestors fled the earthquake in Uzziah’s day (vv. 4–5). Then the LORD comes, “and all the holy ones with him”.
verseByVerse.theology: God lets his people come to the very edge of destruction, and then comes himself, standing on the hill where his Son ascended.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, a day is coming for the LORD, when the spoil taken from you will be divided in your midst. For I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem to battle, and the city shall be taken and the houses plundered and the women raped. Half of the city shall go out into exile, but the rest of the people shall not be cut off from the city. Then the LORD will go out and fight against those nations as when he fights on a day of battle. On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives that lies before Jerusalem on the east, and the Mount of Olives shall be split in two from east to west by a very wide valley, so that one half of the Mount shall move northward, and the other half southward. And you shall flee to the valley of my mountains, for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azal. And you shall flee as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people will be brought to the brink, but then the LORD himself will come to fight for them and open a way of escape.

A day is coming for the LORD. The last chapter of Zechariah begins at the worst possible moment. The city falls, its spoil is shared out inside its walls, women are raped and half the population is deported. The Bible does not soften what happens in war, and God’s people are not exempt from it. Yet even here “the rest of the people shall not be cut off”: a remnant remains.

Who gathers the nations? “I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem”. Does God then approve of plunder and rape? No. He rules even the wicked acts of nations without sharing their guilt, as with Assyria (Isaiah 10:5–12) and the men who crucified Christ (Acts 2:23), and verses 3 and 12 give his verdict on these armies. Scripture names such violence plainly and never excuses it; God sees it, will judge it, and does not look away from those who carry its wounds.

Then the LORD will go out and fight. When everything has been lost, God goes out himself, as he once fought for Israel at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:14). He does not send help; he comes.

His feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives. God stands on the real hill facing Jerusalem from the east, and it splits under him. The split is not merely a display of power; it opens a valley for his people to flee through. The earthquake “in the days of Uzziah” was the one Amos dated his book by (Amos 1:1), still remembered centuries later.

All the holy ones with him. Then the LORD comes with his heavenly host. The New Testament says the same of Christ’s return: he comes “with all his saints” (1 Thessalonians 3:13).

He will come in the same way. Christians cannot read that place name without remembering Jesus. On the Mount of Olives he taught his disciples about his return (Matthew 24:3), and from it he ascended, while two angels told the watching disciples, “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11–12).

Where Christians differ. Some see the city’s capture as the Roman siege of AD 70; dispensational Christians expect a future siege of the earthly city before Christ’s return, and a literal splitting of the hill.

This commentary’s view. The likelier reading is the final assault on God’s people before the Lord comes (see the introduction). The Mount of Olives splitting (v. 4) is then a prophetic picture of him coming in power to the place where he ascended (Acts 1:11), rather than a forecast of an earthquake.

Uncertain wording. Azal (v. 5) is named nowhere else, and where it lay is unknown. The ESV also notes that where it reads “all the holy ones with him”, other Hebrew manuscripts have “with you”. The details of the flight are uncertain; its point is plain.
verseByVerse.note: Uzziah's earthquake struck in the mid-eighth century BC, more than two hundred years before Zechariah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Unique Day and Living Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the LORD comes, history ends not in darkness but in a new day under one King. It is a unique day, known to the LORD, when light comes at evening (vv. 6–7). Living waters flow out from Jerusalem to the eastern and western seas, summer and winter (v. 8). The LORD is king over all the earth, one LORD with one name (v. 9). The land is levelled and Jerusalem lifted high on its site, inhabited and secure, for “there shall never again be a decree of utter destruction” (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends with light at evening, a river that never dries, and one King acknowledged over all the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day there shall be no light, cold, or frost. And there shall be a unique day, which is known to the LORD, neither day nor night, but at evening time there shall be light. On that day living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem, half of them to the eastern sea and half of them to the western sea. It shall continue in summer as in winter. And the LORD will be king over all the earth. On that day the LORD will be one and his name one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the LORD comes, a day dawns that only he knows, with light where darkness was due, a river of life flowing out to the world, and one King over all the earth.

A unique day. A day unlike any other: “at evening time there shall be light”, just when the light should be going.

Known to the LORD. Only God knows its timing. Jesus said the same of his return: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows”, except the Father (Matthew 24:36). Those who have set dates from passages like this have always been wrong.

Living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem. Out of a city with no river comes a river. “Living waters” means flowing, fresh water, running east to the Dead Sea and west to the Mediterranean, and it does not dry up in summer as the local streams did.

The LORD will be king over all the earth. This is the summit of the book and the goal of history in one sentence. Not king in Israel only, or in the hearts of a few: over everything.

The LORD will be one and his name one. The confession of Israel, “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), is finally acknowledged everywhere, with no rival names.

The river and the name in Christ. Ezekiel saw the same river coming out from under the temple (Ezekiel 47:1), and Revelation ends with “the river of the water of life” flowing from God’s throne (Revelation 22:1). On the last day of the Feast of Booths, the feast of verse 16, Jesus stood up in Jerusalem and promised that whoever believes in him would have “rivers of living water” flowing from his heart; John explains that he meant the Spirit (John 7:2, 37–39). And the one name is heard when every tongue confesses “that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:9–11): “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of verse 6 is uncertain; it may mean that the light, cold and frost of ordinary days will cease. “A unique day” is literally “one day”.
verseByVerse.note: “The eastern sea” is the Dead Sea and “the western sea” the Mediterranean (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: The whole land shall be turned into a plain from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem. But Jerusalem shall remain aloft on its site from the Gate of Benjamin to the place of the former gate, to the Corner Gate, and from the Tower of Hananel to the king's winepresses. And it shall be inhabited, for there shall never again be a decree of utter destruction. Jerusalem shall dwell in security.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem will be lifted high above a levelled land and made safe for ever, never again under a sentence of destruction.

Jerusalem shall remain aloft on its site. The country is flattened and the city raised, so that Jerusalem stands out above everything, which is Micah’s picture too (Micah 4:1). Geba, a few miles north of Jerusalem, had long marked Judah’s northern border (2 Kings 23:8), and Rimmon probably lay far to the south in the Negeb (Joshua 15:32).

From the Gate of Benjamin. The gates and towers are named like a surveyor’s list, down to the king’s winepresses: the whole city restored (compare Jeremiah 31:38–40).

There shall never again be a decree of utter destruction. The great words are “never again”. The decree of utter destruction is the Hebrew herem, the ban: things devoted to the LORD for destruction, as the ESV notes. The security is permanent, which nothing in this world has ever been.

The promise kept in Christ. John saw this promise kept in the city God builds, the home of his people in the new creation: “No longer will there be anything accursed” (Revelation 22:3). It can be kept because the curse has already fallen on Christ: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nations that fought God’s city are defeated, their survivors become its worshippers, and all of life is made holy. A rotting plague and a panic from the LORD break the attacking armies, and their wealth is gathered in (vv. 12–15). Then the survivors of those very nations go up year after year to worship the King and keep the Feast of Booths, and any who refuse, Egypt included, receive no rain (vv. 16–19). Finally “Holy to the LORD” is inscribed on the bells of the horses, every pot in Jerusalem and Judah is as holy as the bowls before the altar, and no trader is left in the house of the LORD (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The nations that attacked God's city end up worshipping there, and ordinary life is made holy from the horses' harness upward.

verseByVerse.quote: And this shall be the plague with which the LORD will strike all the peoples that wage war against Jerusalem: their flesh will rot while they are still standing on their feet, their eyes will rot in their sockets, and their tongues will rot in their mouths. And on that day a great panic from the LORD shall fall on them, so that each will seize the hand of another, and the hand of the one will be raised against the hand of the other. Even Judah will fight at Jerusalem. And the wealth of all the surrounding nations shall be collected, gold, silver, and garments in great abundance. And a plague like this plague shall fall on the horses, the mules, the camels, the donkeys, and whatever beasts may be in those camps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who make war on God’s people will be utterly defeated, struck by a plague from the LORD and turned against one another, and their wealth will pass to God’s city.

Their flesh will rot. The judgment is horrifying, described as a body decaying while still upright. The eyes and tongues named are perhaps those used against God, in greed and blasphemy.

A great panic from the LORD. The attacking army turns on itself, as armies in Scripture repeatedly do (Judges 7:22; 2 Chronicles 20:23). This is picture language of utter defeat: no one who sets himself against God can stand.

The wealth of all the surrounding nations. The war machine, animals included, is destroyed, and the wealth of the nations ends up in God’s city, which Haggai had promised in happier terms: “the treasures of all nations shall come in” (Haggai 2:7–8).

Is this too harsh? It is God’s verdict on armies bent on destroying his people, not a licence for anyone’s violence. And in the very next verse their survivors become worshippers.

Uncertain wording. “Even Judah will fight at Jerusalem” may also be read, as the ESV notes, “against Jerusalem”. The first has Judah defending the city; the second, Judah drawn at first into the attack.

verseByVerse.quote: Then everyone who survives of all the nations that have come against Jerusalem shall go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Booths. And if any of the families of the earth do not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, there will be no rain on them. And if the family of Egypt does not go up and present themselves, then on them there shall be no rain; there shall be the plague with which the LORD afflicts the nations that do not go up to keep the Feast of Booths. This shall be the punishment to Egypt and the punishment to all the nations that do not go up to keep the Feast of Booths. And on that day there shall be inscribed on the bells of the horses, "Holy to the LORD." And the pots in the house of the LORD shall be as the bowls before the altar. And every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy to the LORD of hosts, so that all who sacrifice may come and take of them and boil the meat of the sacrifice in them. And there shall no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations that once attacked God’s city will come back year after year to worship its King, and in the end everything, down to horse bells and cooking pots, will be holy to the LORD.

Year after year to worship the King. The survivors of the armies that attacked Jerusalem do not slink away; they come back to worship. Out of the nations that fought him, God takes worshippers.

To keep the Feast of Booths. At the Feast of Booths Israel lived in shelters of branches for a week, remembering that God had brought them through the wilderness living in tents (Leviticus 23:42–43). It was also the harvest festival, a feast of pilgrimage and homecoming, which is exactly what these nations have made.

There will be no rain on them. Refusal has consequences. Egypt is singled out, perhaps because it depended on the Nile rather than rainfall and might have thought itself exempt. Nobody is exempt.

Inscribed on the bells of the horses. “Holy to the LORD” was engraved on the gold plate on the high priest’s turban, the holiest thing a person could wear (Exodus 28:36). Now it is stamped on the bells of the horses, jingling on the harness of working animals in the street.

As the bowls before the altar. The ordinary cooking pots in the house of the LORD become as sacred as the bowls used for sacrificial blood. Then the holiness spreads outward until every pot in Jerusalem and Judah is holy, and pilgrims can walk into any kitchen and use its saucepan to boil the meat of their sacrifice.

There shall no longer be a trader. No one buying and selling holiness, no market in the temple courts. Centuries later Jesus made a whip of cords, drove the traders out of the temple and told them, “do not make my Father’s house a house of trade”; many think this verse was in his mind, and the disciples remembered, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:15–17).

The nations come to the King. That worship has already begun. When some Greeks came up to the feast asking to see Jesus, he said the hour of his glory had come (John 12:20–23). John later saw “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

Holiness for all of life. Zechariah ends where the Bible ends: not a world divided into sacred and ordinary, but one where everything is holy to the LORD. For Christians this begins now, because Christ has made his people “a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5). There is no such thing as a secular Monday; the kitchen, the office and the van are all places where God’s name is worn.

Where Christians differ. Readings of these verses follow views of the millennium (the thousand years of Revelation 20). Dispensational premillennial Christians expect a literal fulfilment after Christ returns: Christ reigning from Jerusalem for a thousand years, the nations coming annually to a rebuilt temple. Historic premillennial Christians also expect an earthly reign then, but many read the temple and feast language less literally. Postmillennial Christians see here the gospel’s wide triumph among the nations before Christ comes. Amillennial Christians read the language as the prophet’s way of describing the reign of Christ now, from heaven, and the worship of all nations, fulfilled in the gospel and completed in the new creation, where the whole earth is the temple.

This commentary’s view. This commentary holds the last view, because the New Testament treats temple, sacrifice and Jerusalem as fulfilled in Christ: Hebrews says the old offerings are finished (Hebrews 10:18) and that believers have already come “to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22), and John saw no temple in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:22). Faithful Christians hold each of these views, and all hold firmly that Christ will return bodily, judge the nations and reign, and that people from every nation will worship him.

Uncertain wording. In verse 18 the ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the word “rain”, so the sentence may simply mean that the same plague falls on Egypt. In verse 21 “trader” may also be read “Canaanite” (ESV note), a word that came to mean a merchant; either way, nothing unholy or mercenary is left in God’s house.

14.title: The LORD Will Be King over All the Earth
14.overview:
Where we are. This last chapter completes the book’s second oracle (chapters 12–14). Chapter 13 ended with the shepherd struck and a refined people saying, “The LORD is my God”; now the prophet looks to the very end, when that God comes in person.

The message. God’s people may be brought to the edge of ruin, but the LORD himself will come, rescue them and reign. History ends not in darkness but in light at evening, a river of life flowing out from his city, and one King over all the earth. The nations that fought him come to worship him, and holiness spreads until the most ordinary things belong to God.

Why it was said. To a tiny community gathered round an unfinished temple in a province of the Persian Empire (see the introduction), promises of a worldwide kingdom could sound absurd. This chapter does not hide that worse lies ahead, but it tells them how the story ends.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD comes (vv. 1–5): the nations take the city, then the LORD goes out to fight, his feet on the Mount of Olives, which splits to open a way of escape. A new day dawns (vv. 6–11): light at evening, living waters, the LORD one and his name one, and the city lifted high and safe for ever. Enemies become worshippers (vv. 12–21): the attacking armies are broken by plague and panic, their survivors go up year after year to keep the Feast of Booths, and “Holy to the LORD” is written on horse bells and cooking pots.

Where it leads. Partly by direct promise and pattern, above all by the character of God revealed in Christ. The LORD whose feet stand on the Mount of Olives is the God who came among us in Jesus: from that hill Jesus ascended, and the angels promised that he “will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). At the Feast of Booths he offered the living water (John 7:37–39); and every tongue will “confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:11). Revelation takes up the river and the end of every curse for the new creation (Revelation 22:1–3).

For us. History is not drifting; it is heading for the day when the LORD is king over all the earth, so God’s people need not despair when the city seems lost. God’s worst enemies can still become his worshippers, so pray for them. And there is no secular corner of life: the kitchen, the van and the office can all bear the words “Holy to the LORD”.
14.theology:
God's people may be brought to the edge of destruction before he intervenes, but then he comes in person, standing on the hill from which his Son ascended and to which he will return, and his power opens a way of escape for his people (vv. 2-5). His timing is his own, and his light comes when the darkness should be falling (vv. 6-7).

From his city flows a river that never dries, begun in Christ and completed in the new creation (v. 8; Ezek 47:1; John 7:38; Rev 22:1), and history ends with the LORD king over all the earth, one LORD and one name (v. 9; Rev 11:15). He takes worshippers out of the nations that fought against him (v. 16), and in the end the division between sacred and ordinary disappears: everything is Holy to the LORD (vv. 20-21).
14.examples: A city falls before God arrives, and a hill splits open to make an escape route. Light comes at evening when darkness was due, and a river runs in both directions out of a city that never had one. Attacking armies come back as pilgrims, the high priest's inscription is stamped on horse bells, ordinary saucepans become as holy as the bowls at the altar, and no market stall is left anywhere in the house of God.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD will be king over all the earth. On that day the LORD will be one and his name one.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the chapter and of the whole book, which began on a building site and ends here. Everything else in the chapter, the rescue, the living waters, the nations worshipping and the holy cooking pots, flows from this one fact: the LORD reigns over all, with no rival. The New Testament hears it fulfilled as every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:11).

14.reflection:
The chapter opens with the city taken before the LORD comes to fight (vv. 1–3). How does it help to know that God’s people may be brought to the edge before he acts? Where do you need to hear “The LORD will fight for you” this week?

From the Mount of Olives Jesus ascended, and the angels promised he would come back in the same way (Acts 1:11). How should the certainty of his return shape the way we live and the way we face the news?

The nations that attacked Jerusalem end up worshipping its King (v. 16). Who seems to you most opposed to God, and how does this promise change the way you pray for them?

“Holy to the LORD” moves from the high priest’s turban to horse bells and cooking pots (vv. 20–21). What ordinary part of your week do you treat as outside God’s claim, and what would it look like to do it as holy to him?
